why.say: Quick game: guess the number. A Demand Package lands on an adjuster's desk. How many pages does she read before she's made up her mind? Shout it out. {name}, three hundred? Bless you. {name}, two? Closer. The honest answer is that the first page or two set the tone, and the rest is checking. A firm I worked with once sent a demand so thick the courier asked if we wanted a dolly. The offer came back tiny, because nobody could find the good stuff. Now two numbers. John Doe's Specials, meaning his bills and lost wages, the damages with a hard number on them, come to $16,401.40. Robert Smith carries $10,000 with Keystone. So what makes Keystone pay all of it, inside 30 days? There's a tool for that, and it has five parts. Miss any one and Keystone can say no and lose nothing. I'm going to reveal them one at a time.
why.ask: {name}, before I reveal anything: what do you think makes an insurance company pay its whole limit, fast?

doc.say: Before you build a demand that asks for it, let's break down a document with a long name and a short job: the affidavit of no other insurance. {name}, guess who signs it: us, John, or the other driver? It's Robert Smith. It's his sworn, notarized statement, sworn meaning under oath, that his Keystone policy is the only liability coverage for this collision: no umbrella, no business or employer's policy, nothing else. Its legal purpose is simple. Atty. Thorne makes it a condition of the demand, because settling at a $10,000 limit needs sworn proof that nothing else covers Smith. Its evidentiary role comes later. Smith swore it on 08/10/2026, Keystone sent it with its tender, its offer to pay the full limit, and both UM carriers reviewed it before they consented. Your handling is the paperwork, never the meaning. You record it in the approved terms, check it's sworn and matches the file, file it with the tender and cite it on page one of each UM demand. The lazy check is "it's notarized." The high-value check is "it's notarized, the names and policy match, and the UM carriers have seen it." Skip that, and a hidden umbrella policy shows up after John already signed.
doc.ask: {name}, why would Harbor Point want to see Smith's affidavit before it consents to the settlement?

theory.say: Here's the tool: a Time-Limited Demand. Plain words, it's a letter that asks for the full policy limit and gives the insurer a set number of days to say yes. The road has five stops. Confirm the foundation, meaning the deadline to sue, who's at fault and how much coverage there is, each from its own document. Demand within limits, with clear terms. Give a reasonable window. Send a package complete enough to judge. And email it to the adjuster, with the clock starting from her written acknowledgement that she got it. Atty. Thorne decides every term. Now four ideas. A demand isn't begging for money; it presents a debt owed. A Time-Limited Demand forces a decision on the record. The Final Scrub catches the adjuster's favorite traps before anything goes out. It's the last line-by-line clean-up before the package leaves: duplicates out, every balance confirmed with the provider, old injuries disclosed, like checking your teeth for spinach before the big meeting. And the fourth is the reason most demands get cut: the Why Factor. Every bill carries the reason the treatment was needed. A bill without a why is just a receipt, and adjusters treat receipts like suggestions.
theory.ask: {name}, where on John Doe's file would a missing Why Factor hurt us most?

frame.say: Three habits sit under every demand we send. Before I show you the first, {name}, guess: once the doctor says the client has healed as much as he's going to, how many days do we give ourselves to send the demand? That moment is called MMI, Maximum Medical Improvement. The answer is thirty, and that's the 30-Day Rule. John Doe reached MMI on 06/12/2026, so the target was 07/12/2026. Ours went out on 07/20/2026, and that's fine, because any later date belongs to Atty. Thorne, with his reason recorded. The lazy version lets the date slide with no note. The high-value version has a late date with a reason on the record. Second, photo impact: we lead with the most graphic image on file, the Property Damage or the injury, because it sets the tone before the adjuster reads a word. Third, the Why Factor again: every bill in the demand carries why that treatment was necessary for his recovery.
frame.ask: {name}, the demand went out eight days after the target. What has to be in the file so nobody calls it a mistake?

rules.say: Here are the rules, and where your role stops. Confirm the foundation first. The deadline to sue, the statute of limitations, is docketed for 02/06/2028. Liability comes from Smith's citation, Ruth Calloway and the doorbell video. Coverage comes from Keystone's $10,000 Dec Page, the policy's summary sheet that shows the limits. The demand is for exactly that $10,000. Every term has to be acceptable as written: Smith and Keystone released, for the BI claim only, BI being the at-fault driver's injury coverage, plus Smith's affidavit, a sworn statement, of no other insurance. Ask only what Keystone can deliver in 30 days, with the Big Four complete. The clock starts at the adjuster's written acknowledgement of receipt, and we email the package to Dana Whitfield. If a statute requires a delivery method, Atty. Thorne confirms it. The gap goes on page one, and causation leads with the 03/13/2026 MRI. Bad faith is a legal conclusion, and it's Atty. Thorne's. In plain words, bad faith means an insurance company unreasonably refusing to pay a claim it should have paid, and whether that happened is never ours to say. You build, audit, serve and prove delivery. You never set terms, grant extensions or value the claim. Why so strict? One vague word gives Keystone a free exit.
rules.ask: {name}, we emailed Dana Whitfield on 07/20, and she confirmed receipt in writing on 07/22. When does the window close, and how would Keystone know?

model.say: Here's the reveal on that window, and the five parts I promised. This is John Doe's demand with the five elements pinned to it. Badge one, the $10,000 amount: within limits. Two, the release and affidavit terms: clear. Three, the conditions and the 30 days to meet them: reasonable. Four, the list of everything enclosed: documented. Five, the deadline and delivery lines: timed. Now the clock bar on the right. Emailed 07/20/2026, receipt confirmed in writing 07/22/2026, and the window closes 08/21/2026. {name}, is that what you got? Keystone knows it because the letter says the clock runs from her written acknowledgement. See the red warning up top? An unclear term is an escape hatch. Each badge is a door Keystone could walk out through, and if we leave one open, they'll walk out holding a lowball offer, like a guy offering to buy your car for the price of its floor mats. This demand shuts all five.
model.ask: {name}, if we'd left one of the five doors open, which do you think Keystone would try first?

job.say: Here's how it runs on the job. MMI is declared on 06/12/2026. You docket MMI plus 30, which means it goes on the calendar with reminders, and you open the Demand Package task in the CMS. That lands on 07/12/2026, a Sunday, and since it's an internal target, we work it early, on Friday 07/10. Legal deadlines counted forward roll to the next business day instead, and a later service date gets recorded as Atty. Thorne's, with his reason. Approved terms go into Case Notes exactly, before you draft a word. When Dana Whitfield confirms receipt in writing on 07/22/2026, you docket 08/21/2026 from that acknowledgement, with reminders. No acknowledgement? Follow up with her that day and escalate to Atty. Thorne; never docket from the send date. A Case Manager I trained once counted from the day she hit send. She landed two days early, and the other side had a field day with it. And if Keystone writes or calls before the deadline, log it word for word and route it to Atty. Thorne the same day. You change nothing on terms or time.
job.ask: {name}, two days pass and no acknowledgement comes back. What exactly do you do, and who hears about it?

dodont.say: Now a game I call Three Clues, One Rule. I'll reveal three clues about something a Case Manager did on this demand. You call it, Do or Don't, then name the rule behind it. {name}, you're keeping score. Here's what's in play. Docketing from the adjuster's written acknowledgement, never the send date. Leading with the value drivers, the facts that make a jury sit up: the MRI herniation, which is a disc pushed out of place, the injection, the numbness and tingling still in his right arm at MMI, and clear liability. Remembering the window is for saying yes, not for paying. And the traps: a demand with no stated deadline, a timeline that leaves the gap out, a demand sent before MMI. If I hear anybody call this a bad-faith letter, I'm stopping you. It's a Time-Limited Demand, and bad faith is Atty. Thorne's conclusion. Now your mystery for the next lesson. Even if Keystone pays every penny of its $10,000, there's a number on this file that says John Doe could walk away with nothing. {name}, find it before I show you.
dodont.ask: {name}, what makes a gap explanation hold up with an adjuster, and who supplies it?

why.say: Would-you-rather, hands up. Would you rather get a check for $10,000, or a check for $6,000 with every bill already paid? {name}, which one? Most people grab the ten. Here's the payoff on our mystery. Take Keystone's $10,000, pull out the fee and costs, and you're at $6,179.92. His liens, the bills that get paid back out of the settlement, are $7,965.00 before anyone reduces them. Do the subtraction, {name}. He walks away with nothing. That's why the UM layers matter so much. UM is his own insurance stepping in when the at-fault driver doesn't carry enough, and it changes his net. Now the uncomfortable part: a technicality can lose them. A release signed too early. A consent nobody got. A consent to settle is the UM carriers' written okay before we settle with the at-fault driver's insurer, and skip it and the client can lose the UM money stacked behind it. A UM demand sent before BI is used up. I once watched a UM claim die because a release got signed on a Friday afternoon so everybody could get it off their desk. This lesson is about locking those escape hatches before Host UM and Relative UM open.
why.ask: {name}, if BI on its own leaves him nothing, what are the UM layers really worth to John Doe?

doc.say: Before you prepare one, let's break down the UM Consent to Settle, and there's a trap in here I'll reveal in a second. It's a UM carrier's written answer to our 30-Day Letter: it consents to the BI settlement, waives subrogation against Robert Smith, which means it gives up its right to chase Smith for what it pays, and says it won't substitute its own check. Its legal purpose is to protect that subrogation right. Here's the trap, {name}: settle and release Smith without it, and John Doe can lose the UM coverage. Its evidentiary role on our file is the green light. Harbor Point consented on 08/24 and Cardinal State on 08/26/2026, each to a release of Smith and Keystone only, with both UM claims left open. Your handling is the process. You prepare both requests for Atty. Thorne's signature, docket each window, file each consent, and nothing goes to John Doe to sign until both are in. The lazy Case Manager waits for one consent and figures the other's coming. The high-value one waits for both, in writing, because one missing letter can cost a client tens of thousands of dollars.
doc.ask: {name}, if Cardinal State still hadn't answered on 08/28, what would happen to the release?

theory.say: Think of UM as the client's financial safety net. Once the at-fault policy is used up, his own coverage makes up the difference, up to its limits. Four ideas hold it together. First, the net check: John Doe doesn't care about the gross, only what's left after fees and unreduced liens. Second, BI exhaustion. Exhaustion just means the at-fault carrier paid every dollar of its limit, and that's the trigger that opens the UM claim as phase two. Third, consent and subrogation waiver. Subrogation is the UM carrier's right to go after the at-fault driver to get its money back. So before we release Smith, the UM carrier consents and gives up that right, or substitutes its own check. Skip that, and the UM claim may not survive the BI release. Fourth, front-load the proof: the at-fault Dec Page, the signed release and the consents go up front, which strips away the technicality defense on page one. The lazy version buries them in an appendix. The high-value version leads with them.
theory.ask: {name}, have you seen a consent-to-settle request on a file before, and what happened when it was missing?

theory2.say: Let's keep going, because a UM claim is a different animal. The UM carrier insures our client, so the claim shifts from third-party, against the other driver's insurer, to first-party, against our client's own insurer. You'd think that makes them friendly. Your own insurer sends you a cheerful renewal email every year, and the day you file a claim, it suddenly needs to verify who you are. It's a contract claim, and it's still a fight. Don't forget that part. UM also doesn't simply pay its limit. It pays the gap between the damages and what's already been collected. Then you need to know the policy's form. An offset policy subtracts the BI money from its UM limit, while add-on or stacked coverage pays on top. And Relative UM sits as excess, meaning it answers only above the primary layers, so the gap it pays starts right where BI and Host UM end. {name}, keep that word excess in your pocket. It comes back.
theory2.ask: {name}, if Harbor Point were an offset policy, how much room would be left on its $20,000 after Keystone's $10,000?

frame.say: Here's how the UM settlement actually gets calculated. Before I build it, {name}, a guess: three policies on this file, $10,000, $20,000 and $10,000. What's the most this file could ever collect for John Doe's injuries? Hold it. Start with total case value, the Medical Bills plus pain and suffering, as Atty. Thorne values them. That number is his, never ours. Subtract the BI settlement, the at-fault driver's maximum limit, which here is Keystone's full $10,000. What's left is the gap, and Harbor Point's Host UM, the coverage on the car he was riding in, covers it up to $20,000. Then comes Relative UM, as excess. Cardinal State answers only above BI and Host UM, so it picks up the gap above $30,000, up to its $10,000 limit. Stack it up and there's your answer, $40,000, but only if the damages are proven above each layer. It's like a three-story building: nobody rents the top floor until the first two are full.
frame.ask: {name}, where does John Doe sit on this ladder right now, and which layer is still waiting to open?

rules.say: These are the rules, and here's where you stop. BI exhaustion comes first: Host UM opens once Keystone's $10,000 tender of 08/12/2026 is documented. A tender is the carrier formally offering its full limit. Prove Keystone is all there is with its Dec Page and Smith's 08/10/2026 affidavit of no other insurance. The day after the tender, 08/13, the 30-Day Letters go to Harbor Point and Cardinal State asking each to consent and waive subrogation, or substitute its own check. Nothing goes to John Doe for signature until both consents are in writing, 08/24 and 08/26, and Atty. Thorne approves the release. Limit that release to Robert Smith, Keystone and the BI claim. Harbor Point confirmed add-on in writing on 03/02/2026; get the same in writing from Cardinal State. You prepare, track, catch and draft. You never interpret a policy or release for John Doe, or tell him to sign. Get the order wrong and $30,000 of safety net can vanish with one signature.
rules.ask: {name}, Keystone's draft release is in your inbox and Dana Whitfield wants it back today. What's wrong with it?

model.say: Picture this as a train line with six stations, and the answer to {name}'s question is on it. One, the tender on 08/12. Two, the consent requests on 08/13. Three, the consents themselves, 08/24 and 08/26. Then comes that heavy orange gate: no release before both consents. Only after it do we reach four, the Limited Release on 08/28. A Limited Release ends only the named claim against the named people, here Robert Smith and Keystone, so the UM claims stay alive. Five, the UM demands on 08/31. Six, Keystone's check on 09/04. Above the rail is the ladder we're protecting: BI $10,000, Host UM $20,000 as add-on, Relative UM $10,000 as excess. And here's the reveal, down in the corner, struck through: the line from Keystone's 08/14 draft, “all other persons, firms, corporations and insurers.” Sign that, and you've released the very carriers we still need money from. It's like selling your house and accidentally signing over the neighbor's too. The lesson of this slide is simple. Sequence is protection.
model.ask: {name}, what would have happened to the stack if station four had come before station three?

job.say: Now let's see how that runs at your desk. Keystone tenders the $10,000 on 08/12/2026. That's your trigger to prepare the 30-Day Letters, the consent-to-settle requests, to both UM carriers for Atty. Thorne's signature, using the template in the Action Plan Editor, and to docket each window. Both go out 08/13 with the tender, the Dec Page and the affidavit. On 08/14, Keystone's draft release arrives. The lazy move is forwarding it to the client with “please sign and return.” The high-value move is comparing who and what it releases against the approved terms and flagging the overbreadth. That “all other insurers” language goes to Atty. Thorne as an escalated task, and nothing goes to John Doe to sign. I once saw a release with “standard language, no changes needed” highlighted in yellow at the top. Nothing in a release is standard. Once both consents are in writing and the Limited Release is signed on 08/28, you open two tracked CMS tasks for the UM demands, each with its carrier, claim number and adjuster.
job.ask: {name}, a release says “standard language” at the top. What do you check before you believe that?

dodont.say: Time for Three Clues, One Rule. I'll reveal three clues, you call Do or Don't, and then you name the rule. {name}, you're scorekeeper. The rules in play: exhaustion proof goes at the front of each UM package. Harbor Point's 03/02/2026 add-on letter goes on the Coverage Matrix. The Coverage Matrix is the chart in the CMS that tracks every policy from reported to confirmed in writing. Cardinal State's form gets confirmed in writing too, so no anti-stacking clause, a rule that stops policies adding together, caps John Doe at $20,000. And the traps: treating Harbor Point and Cardinal State as friendly, letting an “all other insurers” release reach the client, promising full limits early, celebrating $40,000 before the liens are reduced. Consent isn't a courtesy. It protects the UM carrier's subrogation right, which is exactly why releasing Smith without it can cost the coverage. Now your mystery for the next lesson. On 08/05/2026, Keystone looked at our demand and offered $3,500, with exactly two reasons. {name}, before the next lesson, guess both.
dodont.ask: {name}, John Doe is their insured, so why are Harbor Point and Cardinal State now adversaries?

case.say: Let's rewind the calendar. It's Monday, 07/20/2026, and an email just landed from Atty. Thorne. Before I read it, {name}, guess what he wants done today. Here's the reveal: the Keystone BI demand gets a final audit and goes out today. The terms are approved for Dana Whitfield at Keystone Mutual, claim KM-26-440871: the $10,000 limits, a Limited Release of Robert Smith and Keystone only, Smith's affidavit of no other insurance, and 30 days from receipt. MMI was 06/12/2026, Dr. Reyes's Causation Letter and the Gap Explanation Record are on file, and the pre-demand audit put the Specials at $16,401.40. I'm handing you the demand specialist's draft. Fair warning, it has problems. Audit it against the Big Four and the Final Scrub, log every deficiency as a task, and bring it back for his signature. Nothing goes out until the audit is logged. You're the last set of eyes before an adjuster goes looking for a reason to pay less.
case.ask: {name}, before you open the draft, what are the first three things you'll check?

grade.say: Before you touch the draft, look at what an A looks like, because this is the standard the platform audits you against. Five tests decide a Time-Limited Demand: within limits, clear, reasonable, documented and timed. The terms are Atty. Thorne's, word for word. The gap is answered on page one, before Keystone gets to raise it. Inside the package: the cover letter at the $10,000 limit, the liability proof, every itemized bill with its reason, the gap proof, Northgate's wage letter, and the narrative. Build your own version from the case documents you download, in your training Drive, then upload the served set to the CMS. The bare minimum is a package where everything's there. The A is a package where an adjuster can't find a single loose thread to pull. {name}, you're going to tell me which test you'd fail first if you rushed.
grade.ask: {name}, which one of the five tests, if missed, hands Keystone the safest refusal?

task.say: Here's your job. Audit the draft against the Big Four and the Final Scrub in the Action Plan Editor, and log each deficiency as an assigned CMS task rather than fixing it quietly. Assemble the package with the gap answered on page one of the timeline. Once Atty. Thorne signs, email the demand to Dana Whitfield from the Email Workspace with the Demand Package attached, and log it. When her written acknowledgement of receipt comes back dated 07/22/2026, docket the acceptance deadline from it, with reminders. Then you'll take a live call from Dana Whitfield. Confirm receipt and the 08/21/2026 deadline as written, agree to no extension, log her requests in her exact words, and send nothing without approval. {name}, you're taking the first call. {name}, you're logging it. And if she says it's still under review on day two, don't panic. One adjuster I dealt with had a file under review so long it had a birthday. You hand in an audited, emailed demand, her written acknowledgement on file, and 08/21/2026 docketed.
task.ask: {name}, suppose Dana Whitfield emails on day 25 asking for two more weeks. Who answers?

check.say: Before you log anything, check yourself, and I'm going to pick on a few of you. {name}, is the amount $10,000, Keystone's BI limit per its 03/20/2026 Dec Page? Do the terms match Atty. Thorne's approval word for word? Are the Big Four complete, with Specials of $16,401.40 and the Riverton Drug receipts counted once? Did your Final Scrub catch the 05/04/2026 duplicate, taking Riverton Spine & Rehab from $6,290.00 to $6,105.00? Is the gap answered on page one, and are the 2021 low-back visits disclosed as resolved, with no neck history? Disclosed and distinguished, never hidden. Hiding them is the classic lazy move: the adjuster always finds them, and then she trusts nothing else in the package. Every deficiency should be a dated, assigned task. The demand should be emailed 07/20 and logged, and 08/21/2026 docketed from Dana's 07/22 written acknowledgement. If you counted from the send date, you had the right idea and the wrong day. Any extension request goes to Atty. Thorne the same day.
check.ask: {name}, if you docketed from the send date, what day did you land on, and why is it wrong?

audit.say: Here's the enclosure set as the demand specialist built it, and here's your job, {name}: call every item. Keep it, replace it, pull it, add what's missing, or flag it for Atty. Thorne. Some of these are small and some of them cost John Doe real money. Exhibit E carries Riverton Spine and Rehab at six thousand two hundred and ninety dollars with the fourth of May billed twice, and Crescent's statement bills him fifteen hundred and forty dollars that an in-network provider can't bill him at all. In-network means the provider agreed to the insurer's prices, so it can't charge the client the difference. Two things are missing that the letter leans on. A duplicate bill is an adjuster's favorite gift: find one, and she'll politely assume everything else is padded too. When you hand it in you'll see the package as Atty. Thorne actually signed and served it on the twentieth of July, and you can mark your own audit against it. Then the next mystery: the BI round ends, and two more carriers are waiting.
audit.ask: {name}, which item in this set would you least want Dana Whitfield to find first?

case.say: Look at the date first. It's Monday, 08/31/2026, and something we've been waiting for still isn't here. {name}, guess what. Keystone's check. Here's what landed from Atty. Thorne. BI is done: Keystone tendered $10,000 on 08/12 after Smith's affidavit of 08/10. Harbor Point consented on 08/24, Cardinal State on 08/26, and the Limited Release of Robert Smith and Keystone was signed 08/28. He wants the Host UM demand to Harbor Point for $20,000 and the Relative UM demand to Cardinal State for $10,000, as excess, with exhaustion on page one of each and the response deadline left blank for him. And remember, on 08/05 Keystone leaned on the 14-day gap and called the MRI degenerative. Expect the UM carriers to try the very same thing. Adjusters share arguments the way teenagers share homework.
case.ask: {name}, with no check in hand today, what proves exhaustion?

grade.say: Here is the standard for the two UM packages. They are two separate packages for two carriers, never the BI demand with a new address on it. I once saw a UM demand go out with the BI adjuster's name still in the greeting. The UM adjuster pinned it to her wall, and not as a compliment. Each one opens with the proof of exhaustion: Keystone's tender, its Declaration Page, Smith's affidavit, both consents and the signed Limited Release. Then coverage, liability and damages. Cardinal State's demand is framed as excess, for damages above thirty thousand. A two-page treatment summary beats a stack of records. The response deadline stays blank, because Atty. Thorne sets it. Build both drafts from the documents in your training Drive, tie every figure to its source, and upload them to the CMS with a follow-up task on each. {name}, you're the one checking the greeting lines.
grade.ask: {name}, why does exhaustion go on page one rather than in an appendix?

task.say: You're not starting from a blank page. The audit closed on 07/15, and Atty. Thorne assigned the UM demands to the Demand Desk; their drafts are in the file. Your job is QC, quality control. Host UM goes to Marcus Bell at Harbor Point, HP-26-7741, for the $20,000 limit; Relative UM goes to Teresa Okafor at Cardinal State, CS-26-20355, for $10,000 as excess over Host UM. Exhaustion is proven by the tender, the consents and the signed Limited Release, with the check copy to follow, and it belongs on page one of each. Check every figure against the audit, answer the gap and “degenerative” with the MRI, and hand in two QC'd drafts routed to Atty. Thorne. {name}, you take Harbor Point. {name}, you take Cardinal State. Then swap and check each other's, because fresh eyes catch what tired eyes skip.
task.ask: {name}, why does Cardinal State's demand say excess?

check.say: Quick term first: an impairment rating is the doctor's percentage for how much permanent loss of function is left, and only a doctor gives one. Check your two packages before you route them. {name}, are they truly two, each complete on its own? Cardinal State gets the whole file, not a cross-reference to Harbor Point's. Is Relative UM framed as excess, claimed for damages above $30,000? Is exhaustion on page one of each: the 08/12 tender, Keystone's 03/20 Dec Page, Smith's 08/10 affidavit, the consents, the 08/28 release, and a task for the check copy? Are the 03/02 and 03/09 coverage letters in? Does your gap section answer “degenerative” with the radiologist's own words, “no significant degenerative change at the adjacent levels”? If it doesn't, you haven't learned from the BI round. Is there a two-page treatment summary instead of a record dump? And is the response deadline a marked blank for Atty. Thorne, with nothing served? Now your mystery. We keep saying Keystone leaned on the gap on 08/05. In the next practice you'll hear exactly how she said it, live, on the phone.
check.ask: {name}, does Dr. Reyes's MMI note carry an impairment rating, and if not, what do you ask Atty. Thorne?

questions.say: Learning Check, game-show edition. The questions are on the screen, and your answers come from this file, in your own words, typed right under each question. Here's the twist: when you're done, I'll pull names, and you defend one answer out loud as if Dana Whitfield were on the line. {name}, you might be first. State the BI demand's terms, how it was served and the date its window closed, and show me how you counted. Name the five elements, with this file's example of each, and tell me who decides bad faith. Then answer Keystone's degenerative and gap arguments with the documents, and say where each goes in the package. When you reach the pressure questions, I want the process, not the law. Use the file's own dates and figures, not general rules. No phoning a friend, and definitely no phoning an adjuster.
questions.ask: {name}, before you start, what does a UM carrier's consent actually protect?

summary.say: Now the Self-Summary. In your own words, write what you learned serving John Doe's demands, the principles that make a demand hold, not the clicks. Then your strategy: with both UM drafts on Atty. Thorne's desk on 08/31/2026, what's your next action, and why that one? And name the one thing you're least confident about. Before anyone writes, look at the scenario on screen. Keystone's draft release arrives 08/14/2026 releasing all other insurers, Harbor Point hasn't answered the consent request, and Atty. Thorne is out until Monday. I've lived this one. A Case Manager I worked with got that exact kind of release on a Friday, with the adjuster calling every hour saying they just needed it back today. She held it, flagged it, and that patience kept the client's UM claim alive. {name}, talk us through what you'd do first.
summary.ask: {name}, with Atty. Thorne out until Monday, what must not happen to Keystone's release before he's back?

scale.say: Last step for this module, the Skill Scale. Rate yourself 1 to 5 on each competency, from docketing a Time-Limited Demand from receipt all the way to holding the UPL boundary on terms, extensions and releases. UPL is the unauthorized practice of law, giving legal advice when you're not a lawyer. Be honest with yourself. A self-rating isn't a dating profile; nobody's impressed by all fives. I'm going to compare your rating with your score, and a 5 on a block scored at 60 is a conversation, just like a 2 on a block you aced. And remember, UPL is a gate. A strong score doesn't survive an ethics breach. When you're done, submit it for review. {name}, a teaser for the negotiation check coming up: there's one number on this file that comes out the same every time you do the math on a lowball. Find it.
scale.ask: {name}, where's the widest gap between how you rated yourself and how you actually scored?

why.say: Quick game: finish the sentence. I start something an adjuster always says, you finish it. “We're still…” {name}? Reviewing, yes. “I'll have to check with…” My supervisor, of course. I've never met the supervisor, but I hear he's extremely busy. Now the payoff from the last lesson. Here's the six-word question Dana Whitfield is going to ask, not the one we'd like her to ask: “Why did he wait two weeks?” Answer me from documents only. No adjectives. Here's the reality of this file. Keystone won't argue the crash. Robert Smith was cited, and the doorbell camera caught him. So it'll argue the 14-Day Gap, it'll call the MRI degenerative, and it'll stall toward 08/21/2026. A Case Manager who has mapped both attacks, and the documents that answer them, before the first call turns every stall into a record. That's what today is about.
why.ask: {name}, “Why did he wait two weeks?” Which documents answer her, with no adjectives?

theory.say: In personal injury, the demand letter is your opening move, and adjusters protect the carrier by valuing claims low. So negotiation is prepared, never made up on the spot. Four ideas carry it. The pitch: a demand that reads like a template gets treated like one, while a tailored presentation earns a real evaluation. Value drivers: the few facts that would scare a jury, because they create the carrier's risk, so every call leads with them. Anticipate the response: name your top two weak spots before the adjuster does, and have the documents in hand. And the professional pause. After a low number, stay quiet. Silence shifts the burden back, and the adjuster has to justify the figure with data. It's the longest four seconds of your career. Count them in your head; I once heard a trainee whisper “one Mississippi” into the phone. And remember, this isn't a used-car lot. Nobody's going to go talk to their manager and come back with free undercoating.
theory.ask: {name}, how long do you think you could hold a silence on a call before you cracked?

frame.say: Here's the battle map, four steps, built before any phone rings. {name}, before I show it, guess which step new Case Managers skip the most. Step one, create a Net Sheet. Total the liens, costs and attorney's fee, because below that line the client receives $0. Step two, identify the value drivers, three facts that would scare a jury, and every call leads with them. Step three, anticipate the adjuster's response: name your top two weak spots and the documents that justify them. Step four, prepare the rebuttal so it's ready before she ever brings it up. The answer is step one. People skip the math because it feels like the attorney's job. The decision is his, but the numbers are ours. On John Doe's file, the weak spots aren't a mystery. It's the gap and the degenerative MRI, every single time.
frame.ask: {name}, on John Doe's file, which three facts would scare a jury the most?

rules.say: These are the rules, and where your authority ends. The net floor is liens plus costs plus fee. $7,965.00 plus $486.75 is $8,451.75, and grossing that up for the one-third fee gives $12,677.63. Grossing up just means working out how big the settlement must be so that much is left after the fee. That's above Keystone's whole $10,000 limit, so every layer matters. Lead with the value drivers: Smith on video with an independent witness, the C5-C6 herniation and injection, residual right-arm paresthesia, the numbness and tingling, at MMI. Anchor on $16,401.40 in total Specials, never PIP's $5,000. Soft lead on the call, restate the demand and its 08/21/2026 deadline, then pause and ask for her data. Name every stall. Keystone's $3,500 is a counteroffer, logged in her exact words, and whether it ended the demand is Atty. Thorne's call. You present, ask, restate and relay. You never counter, move the number or the deadline, or tell John Doe what an offer's worth.
rules.ask: {name}, if this file settled for Keystone's full $10,000 and nothing else, what would John Doe net?

model.say: Here's the reveal, {name}: on unreduced liens, he nets $0. This is the battle map for Keystone, finished before the phone rings. Station one is the net floor, $12,677.63 gross, with that red note reminding you Keystone's limit is only $10,000. Station two holds the value drivers. Station three is their top two attacks in red, the 14-day gap and the “degenerative” MRI. And station four answers each one with a source: the EMS report and the 06/19/2026 Causation Letter, the doctor's letter tying the injury to the crash, for the gap, and the Summit MRI of 03/13/2026 for degenerative. Up in the corner, the demand expires 08/21/2026. The lazy Case Manager walks into that call with a hunch. The high-value one walks in with a card for every attack. Every attack on this file has a document waiting for it before she dials.
model.ask: {name}, if she opens with the gap, which card on station four do you read from first?

job.say: Here's how it plays out on the job. Keystone receives the demand on 07/22/2026, and that's your trigger to build the battle map and compute the net floor on the Net Sheet: $12,677.63 gross on unreduced liens, with every attack matched to a dated document in Case Notes. When the adjuster calls with an offer, you soft-lead, pause, ask for her data and restate the approved demand. You'll practice exactly that in the Call Simulator against Dana Whitfield. No counter, terms and deadline unchanged. When the call ends, log the offer and her exact words in the Communications Log and report to Atty. Thorne that day. And if she stalls with “waiting on authority,” you name it and send a same-day email citing 08/21/2026. No open-ended callbacks. I once watched an adjuster crawl from $3,500 to $3,550 to $3,600 over three weeks. It was like watching a glacier haggle. What finally moved things wasn't patience; it was a dated email that put the deadline in writing and went straight to the attorney.
job.ask: {name}, she says “I'll get back to you.” What's your next sentence, and what goes out by email today?

dodont.say: Let's play Three Clues, One Rule. I'll reveal three clues, you call Do or Don't, and you name the rule. {name}, you're on the buzzer first. Here's the territory. Making the adjuster justify her number with data, and using silence after a low offer. Staying firm, factual and professional, because an angry call is a gift to the carrier. Personalizing every answer to John Doe's record. And the traps: softening the demand to seem reasonable, negotiating without knowing the net floor, anchoring on PIP's $5,000, Specials that don't reconcile to the ledger, accepting “I'll get back to you.” One thing I'll be listening for: nobody apologizes for the gap. It's already explained, by the EMS report, the call-outs, the receipt, the numbness and the Causation Letter. Keep your tone flat and factual. Now your mystery for the next lesson. There's one sentence in a letter from one of John Doe's own carriers that's worth $10,000 to him. The letter is dated 03/02/2026. {name}, find the sentence.
dodont.ask: {name}, what's the difference between holding the demand and softening it to seem reasonable?

why.say: Treasure hunt. I've got Harbor Point's 03/02/2026 letter up, and somewhere in it is the sentence worth $10,000 to John Doe. {name}, you've had since the last lesson. Where is it? Give it a second. It's the add-on clause. Add-on means Harbor Point pays on top of what Keystone pays. On a reduction policy, Keystone's $10,000 would have come straight off the top of the $20,000. One sentence, ten thousand dollars. That's why we read insurance letters the way a detective reads a ransom note. Once Keystone tenders, the money that makes John Doe whole sits with two first-party carriers that insure him, and both of them will argue against him. We reach $40,000 by proving the gap above each layer, closing every reduction in writing first, and papering every single move.
why.ask: {name}, without that add-on sentence, what would Harbor Point's $20,000 have shrunk to?

theory.say: A UM settlement is won on paper. The package shows the other driver's fault, and it shows that the damages are more than what's been collected. Compare a weak file with a legal trap. Raw charts and a casual letter carry no risk for the carrier, while a clear summary on a clock raises it. Sort documents by function, coverage, liability and damages, and let the diagnostics and a causation narrative answer any “he had this before” defense. You'll hear about bracketing, paired ranges that build a bridge across a gap and then close in the middle. That's haggling, and Atty. Thorne makes every move there. And PIP, the client's own coverage for Medical Bills, depends on the state. In a no-fault state, PIP is mandatory and pays first, whoever caused the crash; suing needs an injury that passes a threshold, and PIP paid is set off. In an at-fault state, the at-fault driver's BI pays, and add-on PIP pays on top. John Doe's Harbor Point PIP is add-on. {name}, I'll want that back from you in one sentence.
theory.ask: {name}, in a no-fault state, what would John Doe need before he could sue Robert Smith at all?

frame.say: Here's what goes inside a UM demand packet, in four groups, and one group is the first thing a UM carrier looks for. {name}, guess which before I get there. Evidence of liability: the Police Report, Property Damage photos, witness statements, any dashcam or surveillance footage. On our file, that's the citation, Ruth Calloway and the doorbell video. Economic damages: itemized Medical Bills, complete records, lost-wage verification and future medical estimates. Non-economic damages, meaning the pain and how life changed: the demand letter, the client's impact statement and photos of injuries. And proof of exhaustion: the signed Limited Release, the check copy, the at-fault Dec Page and the consent to settle. That's the one they look for first. Get it wrong and the rest barely matters. A UM adjuster with no exhaustion proof is like a bouncer with no ID in front of him. You're not getting in, no matter how good the outfit is.
frame.ask: {name}, which of the four groups was still incomplete on John Doe's file on 08/31/2026?

rules.say: Here are the rules, and where you stop. UM pays the gap: damages as Atty. Thorne values them, minus the BI, up to its limit. Cardinal State's file has to show damages above $30,000. Check the offset rule first; Harbor Point's 03/02/2026 letter answers the limit half of “BI already compensated him,” and the medical proof answers the damages half. Both carriers turn adversarial at evaluation, so the first offer is rarely the last. Bracketing is Atty. Thorne's tool alone. When a carrier offers limits, confirm coverage, release scope, liens, payee and check date without accepting, and report that day. Never accept verbally under pressure. John Doe's Harbor Point PIP is add-on, and here it creates no lien and no UM cut. You assemble, log, relay and paper John Doe's decision. You never accept, reject, counter, explain offset language to him, or accuse a carrier of bad faith. The lazy reply on the phone is “sounds great, I'll tell the client.” The high-value one is “thank you, I'll confirm that in writing and get it to Atty. Thorne today.”
rules.ask: {name}, Harbor Point insures Kevin Alvarez's car. Why does it owe John Doe anything, and why will it still fight him?

model.say: This slide shows what could shrink the gross, and where this file actually stands. Three rungs build left to right: BI at $10,000, tendered 08/12, then Host UM at $20,000, then Relative UM at $10,000, with the running total going from $10,000 to $30,000 to $40,000 gross. Under the Host UM rung you'll see three reductions struck through in red: a BI offset, PIP non-duplication, which means not paying twice for the same bill, and a PIP lien. None of them apply. Here's the fun part, {name}: one document knocks out all three. Off to the side sits a reminder that this PIP is add-on, so there's no set-off. Along the bottom is what we confirm before anything's accepted: scope, release, liens, payee and check date, then a confirming email. One letter doing the work of three arguments. That's the best kind of paperwork there is.
model.ask: {name}, which single document knocks out all three red chips, and how does it do it?

job.say: Let's run it on the calendar. On 09/14/2026, Harbor Point's offer comes in. You log the offer and its stated reasons in the Negotiation Log on the Insurance tab and report it to Atty. Thorne that day. Because the offer cites the BI payment and the gap, you assemble a counter-package for his approval: the 03/02/2026 letter, the MRI read, the Causation Letter, the MMI residuals, meaning what's still wrong after healing, and future care. He approves, and it goes out 09/16. When a carrier offers limits, you confirm the terms without accepting and draft the acceptance email, which goes only after John Doe's decision is logged and Atty. Thorne approves. And when each UM check arrives, you confirm its release is signed and deposit it to trust, the firm's account that holds client money, that day: 10/05 and 10/13/2026. True story: I once found a settlement check in a desk drawer, under a takeout menu, three weeks after it arrived. Same day. Every time.
job.ask: {name}, a UM check arrives and you can't find the signed release in the file. What do you do with the check?

dodont.say: Three Clues, One Rule, last round for the lessons. {name}, you're on the buzzer. In play this time: hunting down every stacking and resident-relative policy, because that's why this file reaches $40,000. Getting offset and reimbursement status in writing, the way Harbor Point's 03/02/2026 letter does. Setting John Doe's expectations on the UM timeline without ever promising him a limit. And the traps: taking the first offer because it's his own coverage, promising limits before the offset rule is checked, a bracket move with nothing back from the carrier, a verbal deal with no confirming email, finding a lien after the money's paid out. And anyone who writes the words “bad faith” to an adjuster has crossed the line. That's Atty. Thorne's conclusion to draw. Now the mystery that kicks off our practice. The demand specialist's draft of the Keystone demand is sitting in the file with mistakes in it, one worth $185 and one worth $1,540. {name}, you're hunting both down next.

Keystone offers $3,500.00 to resolve the bodily injury claim. On $16,401.40 in Specials. That's not an offer, that's a coupon. Her reasons: John Doe waited two weeks before seeking any treatment, and the MRI findings are degenerative in nature. She's calling this afternoon. Keep the facts in front of you. Keystone received the $10,000 Time-Limited Demand on 07/22, and acceptance runs to 08/21/2026. Atty. Thorne's written authority says restate the Limits Demand and the deadline, present the record, no counter, and report any offer to him the same day. Now imagine she opens like this: “He waited two weeks. That's not a herniation, that's a 34-year-old's spine.” Who wants to answer her?

Thorne today for him to convey to John Doe, and draft the 08/06/2026 rebuttal for his approval. That's what you hand in. {name}, you're on the phone first. {name}, you're timing the pause. Under three seconds and we go again.

The high-value call reads.

If you dialed without knowing that, you were negotiating blind. Did you pause and ask what data supports $3,500? Did you answer the gap with dated documents, and degenerative with Dr. Park's own sentence? Did you restate $10,000 and 08/21/2026 with no new figure? If you said “let me see what I can do,” or named a number, that's a fail, because the authority was written down so nobody improvises it. Is the offer logged in her exact words, reported on 08/05, with the rebuttal drafted for 08/06? Now your mystery for the next practice. Weeks from now, one of John Doe's own carriers makes the same gap argument, plus a brand-new one. Guess the new one.

case.say: Here's today's landing, 09/14/2026, from Marcus Bell on HP-26-7741. Remember the new argument I asked you to guess? {name}, what did you come up with? Harbor Point offers $8,000.00 on the Host UM claim. His reasons: John Doe didn't treat for two weeks after the accident, and the BI payment has already compensated him for much of this loss. That second one is the new one. He wants to know your client's position. I've put his reasons on the board right beside Harbor Point's own letter of 03/02/2026. Take a good look before anyone drafts a word. The carrier's argument is answered by its own paper. That's my favorite kind of rebuttal, because nobody can argue with their own letterhead. For context, Keystone's $10,000 has been in trust since 09/04, and both UM demands went out on 08/31.

That's the CMS record of every offer, counter and stated reason, with dates, so anyone can pick up the file and see exactly where the money stands. Log Harbor Point's $8,000 with its stated reasons and report it to Atty. Thorne the same day. Whenever a carrier offers or tenders, record John Doe's informed decision through Atty. Thorne, then draft the confirming email in the Email Workspace for his approval, covering coverage, release, liens, payee and check date. You'll finish by proving $40,000.00 gross on the Recovery Ledger in the Net Sheet. The Recovery Ledger is the part of the Net Sheet that adds up every dollar actually recovered, before fees and bills come out. {name}, you're running Harbor Point's log. {name}, you've got Cardinal State.

Does the counter-package answer the offset half with the 03/02/2026 letter and the damages half with the medical proof, including the MMI residuals and future care of $3,400 to $6,800? Did it go out 09/16 with no figure below limits from you? For Harbor Point's $20,000 on 09/29 and Cardinal State's $10,000 tender on 10/06, is each acceptance recorded as John Doe's informed decision through Atty. Thorne, with who, on whose advice, and when? “Accepted” alone is the lazy entry, and it's incomplete. Your Recovery Ledger should read $40,000.00 and nothing else. Add PIP's $5,000 or Keystone's Property Damage payments and you've mixed in money that doesn't belong. Here's the mystery for the Learning Check: $40,000 sounds like a happy ending. Is it?
