questions.say: Here's the Learning Check for the negotiation module, and the number I teased is $0.00, John Doe's net on every lowball. Game-show rules again: answers come from this file, in your own words, typed under each question, and I'll pull names for a lightning round at the end. {name}, stretch now. First, run the math check on Keystone's $3,500: fee, costs, unreduced liens, net. Tell me what it shows Atty. Thorne and who tells John Doe. That's the big question, so show the $0.00 cleanly. Second, answer Dana Whitfield's gap and degenerative arguments with four documents and the radiologist's own words. Third, explain what PIP's $5,000, exhausted and non-subrogated, meaning used up with no right to be paid back, means for valuation, and what would change in a no-fault state. Careful there, because “no set-off here” isn't the same thing as “no reduction anywhere.”
questions.ask: {name}, why is this file free of reductions, and which document says so?

summary.say: Now your Self-Summary. Write what you learned negotiating John Doe's file, the principles rather than the clicks. Then your strategy: if a carrier's offer landed today, what's your next action, and why is it the right one rather than a counter? Then the one thing you're least confident about. Before anyone writes, here's a pressure question out loud. The offer dies at 5:00 p.m. and Atty. Thorne is unreachable. Turn to your neighbor, talk it through for a minute, and then write. A hint from the field: offers that expire at 5:00 have a funny way of still being alive at 5:01 once someone with authority calls back. That's not a reason to ignore the deadline. It's a reason to escalate it, in writing, right now. {name}, you and your neighbor go first. Keep the scenario on screen in mind as well.
summary.ask: {name}, the offer dies at 5:00 p.m. and Atty. Thorne is unreachable. What do you say?

scale.say: Okay, the Skill Scale, and the last thing for today. Give yourself a 1 to 5 on each of the six competencies, from building the battle map and net floor through to holding the authority line, where every number and decision runs through Atty. Thorne. I'll set your self-rating next to your score, and if they're far apart in either direction, we'll talk about it. That's coaching, not a penalty. Just keep in mind that UPL is a gate, so a strong score can't rescue an ethics breach. Submit it for review when you're finished. Now tomorrow's mystery. We just collected $40,000 gross. John Doe's liens are still sitting at $7,965.00, unreduced, and tomorrow we negotiate those bills. {name}, come in with your best guess: how much of that $40,000 actually ends up in John Doe's pocket, and who decides how it gets split?
scale.ask: {name}, which of the six competencies would you most want to practice again before your next file?

why.say: Guessing game, gut answers only, no calculators. How many liens are on John Doe's $40,000? Hands up for one. Now two. Now three or more. {name}, you went for two, didn't you? Most rooms do. Here's the reveal: two asserted and five checked, each one written down with its source. A lien, quick reminder, is a bill with a legal right to be paid out of the settlement before the client gets his share. And liens are like glitter. You think you got them all, and six months later one turns up on the couch. That $40,000 isn't John Doe's until every claim on it is found, sorted and resolved in writing. They don't all bend the same way, either. A statutory lien bends to a formula, a Health Plan's right bends to a doctrine, and a provider's balance bends to a negotiation. Sort one wrong and you either overpay it, which is John's money gone, or freeze the whole payout. In a minute I'll show you which lien on this file is worth the most to get right.
why.ask: {name}, counting the ones we checked and found absent, how many claims did we have to look at on John Doe's $40,000?

theory.say: The legal muscle behind a lien decides how far it'll bend, so picture a ladder. Top rung, the easiest: medical providers who treated on an LOP, a Letter of Protection, which is our written promise that they get paid from the settlement. They're very negotiable, because they'd rather be paid now than wait. Next rung: health insurance subrogation, which just means a private plan wants back what it paid. That's moderate, and it's shaped by two doctrines, made whole and common fund, which Atty. Thorne argues, not us. Made whole means, in many states, the insurer gets paid back only once the client has been fully compensated, and common fund means a lienholder that did none of the work should share the cost of getting the money, like a roommate chipping in for the pizza they're eating. Lower down: Medicare and Medicaid, government payers with strict formulas, and slower than a calculator with a dying battery. Bottom rung: ERISA plans, self-funded employer plans under federal law, notoriously hard to reduce. The lazy Case Manager calls every lienholder and asks for a discount. The high-value one knows which rung each lien sits on before dialing, because that's where the leverage lives. {name}, if you could only make one call today, which rung would you start on?
theory.ask: {name}, which of these lien types have you run into before, and which one gave you the hardest time?

frame.say: Before I show you where John Doe's two liens sit on this chart, {name}, place a bet: is Peach State an ERISA plan or not? Hold your answer. Here's the chart. Medical providers, doctors or hospitals treating on a Letter of Protection, sit high; they often take a reduction to get paid now. Health insurance, private insurers looking for their money back, sits moderate, subject to made whole or common fund. Medicare and Medicaid, the government programs, sit low, with strict formulas and slow processing. ERISA plans, self-funded employer Health Plans, sit very low, governed by federal law and notoriously hard to reduce. Now the reveal. Riverton Spine & Rehab is our LOP provider, top of the ladder. And Peach State is a fully insured Health Plan, not ERISA. Fully insured means the employer bought an insurance policy for its workers instead of paying claims out of its own pocket, so state law, not the federal ERISA rules, generally decides how its payback gets reduced, and Atty. Thorne confirms it. That one fact changes how hard this fight is. If you'd guessed ERISA and treated it that way, you'd have surrendered before the first phone call.
frame.ask: {name}, where do Riverton Spine & Rehab and Peach State land on this chart, and why does it matter for John Doe's net?

rules.say: Here are the rules, and where your role stops. Statutory liens, like Medicare, Medicaid, a hospital lien or workers' comp, come from the law and bend least; contractual claims rest on an agreement. Inventory every claimant, absent ones included. The lazy version writes “no Medicare lien.” The high-value version writes where you checked and when. Two liens are asserted, Peach State and Riverton Spine & Rehab, and every “none” gets its source. Not every payer is a lienholder: Harbor Point's PIP has no reimbursement right, and Crescent Pain & Spine can't balance-bill, meaning it can't send John Doe the leftover. Peach State is fully insured, and what follows is Atty. Thorne's call. He asked for the one-third common-fund share, so $1,860.00 minus $620.00 is $1,240.00. Made whole, comparative fault and quantum meruit are doctrines you can name, never choose. Comparative fault cuts a recovery by the client's own share of the blame, and quantum meruit means getting paid fairly for the work actually done. You classify, gather, audit and draft. You never compromise a lien without his authority, or tell John Doe a lien is invalid.
rules.ask: {name}, Peach State paid $1,860.00 on a $3,400.00 injection. Who can come after John Doe for the other $1,540.00?

model.say: Nobody can, by the way, because Crescent took the contract rate. {name}, if you said nobody, take a bow. Now, this slide sorts every claim on John Doe's $40,000. The ladder runs from most negotiable at the top, the provider LOP, through fully insured Health Plans and workers' comp, down to Medicare and Medicaid, with ERISA self-funded at the bottom. Only two bars are solid: Riverton Spine & Rehab at $6,290.00 and Peach State at $1,860.00. Every other bar is hollow, with a green check saying none, verified. I love those hollow bars. Each one is a lien that tried to sneak in through the back door and got stopped by somebody with a clipboard. There's an outlined prior-attorney bar tagged quantum meruit, which is a lawyer's claim to be paid for work already done, and three doctrine cards, common fund, made whole and comparative fault, with that last one greyed out. And the warning along the bottom: unclassified means overpaid or frozen.
model.ask: {name}, why do you think the comparative fault card is greyed out on John Doe's file?

job.say: Let's put it on the job. When the gross reaches $40,000.00 on 10/06/2026, you run the final inventory in the Lien Tracker, re-verifying the Day 2 register, asserted and absent, and classifying each claim as statutory or contractual. Two stay open; Medicare, Medicaid, hospital, workers' comp and PIP each get “none” with a source, and the prior attorney gets “none known to John Doe”. Once the Health Plan lien is classified, you get the plan documents and escalate the funding status to Atty. Thorne. Fully insured goes on file, and the governing-law call is recorded as his. When he picks the reduction basis, you draft the request naming the doctrine and showing $1,860.00 minus $620.00 equals $1,240.00, held for his approval. And for the prior-attorney question, ask John Doe, check intake, and log “no other lawyer known to John Doe” with its date and source.

dodont.say: Here comes Three Clues, One Rule. I reveal three clues, you call Do or Don't, then name the rule. The rules in play: work the most negotiable lien first to build momentum, but resolve every one in writing before disbursement. Record a verified “none” the way you'd record a lien, with its source and date. Name the doctrine and show the math in every Reduction Request. And the traps: treating an ERISA plan like a provider LOP, asking for a courtesy discount with no legal basis, paying a prior attorney a percentage he's no longer owed. One heads-up. Someone will ask whether riding in Kevin Alvarez's carpool makes this workers' comp. That's a coverage question for Atty. Thorne. We record that no claim was filed and no lien asserted.
dodont.ask: {name}, john Doe knows of no other lawyer. Why does quantum meruit still get a line in the Lien Tracker?

why.say: I've covered the last row of this table. It shows what would have happened with only Keystone's $10,000 BI. Quick vote with your thumbs: up if John Doe takes home more than a few thousand, sideways if it's a little, down if it's nothing. {name}, where's your thumb? Here's the reveal: $0.00. That's why this lesson exists. And if your palms started sweating when I said math, relax. You don't have to love math. You need a calculator and the patience to use it twice. Half the job is getting money from the carriers. The other half is keeping it from the lienholders, because every dollar a lien gives up lands in John Doe's net. And what moves a provider isn't a plea for a favor. It's an honest audit and the pro-rata math, laid out so plainly the provider can check it themselves.
why.ask: {name}, before I uncovered that row, what did you think John Doe would take home on BI alone?

theory.say: Here's the road to reducing the liens, in plain words. First, audit each bill line by line and get any errors corrected before you ask for a reduction. Then run the pro-rata math. Then ask, with Atty. Thorne's written request and his target number. Pay nothing without a full-and-final Payoff Letter. And update the ledger the day a reduction is confirmed. Now the ideas behind it. An error earns a demand for correction, not a favor. Upcoding means billing a fancier visit than the records show, and unbundling means splitting one service into several bills. Pro-rata distribution means that when there's not enough money for everyone, each lien gets a slice in proportion to its size. And the common fund doctrine says a lienholder shouldn't ride free on the work and costs that created the money it's being paid from. {name}, which of these sounds most like something you've seen on a real bill?
theory.ask: {name}, have you ever caught a billing error that the provider fixed without an argument?

frame.say: Here's the path from the bill to the payoff, and remember that mystery charge on Riverton's ledger, because it's coming. Step one, cross-reference the records against the bill, so a Level 3 visit billed as Level 5 gets corrected, not discounted. Step two, hunt for duplicate charges, especially overlapping dates between hospital stays and separate doctor groups. Step three, the common fund. In many states a lienholder reduces by its share of fees and costs, and that's Atty. Thorne's argument to make. Step four, the Payoff Letter. Never pay without a signed letter saying it's full and final satisfaction of the lien. The lazy Case Manager skips straight to step three and asks for a percentage off. The high-value one starts at step one, because every error you find is money you never have to negotiate for. {name}, on John Doe's file, step two has already found something. Any guesses?
frame.ask: {name}, what did the duplicate check find on Riverton Spine & Rehab's ledger?

rules.say: Here's the reveal, and the rules. Audit before you ask: corrections first, reductions second. Riverton billed 34 lines at $185.00, $6,290.00, but the records show 33 visits and a duplicate on 05/04/2026, so you negotiate from $6,105.00. Match each code to that day's note; nothing may fall between 04/02 and 04/21/2026. With only the BI, $6,179.92 would split pro rata, Peach State $1,443.15 and Riverton $4,736.77, and John Doe nets nothing. But on Track A the fund covers both liens, so argue true facts only. The lazy ask is “can you knock some off?” The high-value ask is “here's your bill, here's the duplicate, here's the corrected balance, here's the math.” Never say a provider would take only a share or that the client will refuse the settlement. Common fund is Atty. Thorne's argument. Send his approved request, call with his target, and remember, no Payoff Letter means no payment. You never offer or accept outside his authority.
rules.ask: {name}, Riverton billed $6,290.00. What number do you negotiate from, and why that one?

model.say: Here's the pro-rata picture, on BI alone. That long bar is the $6,179.92 left after fee and costs, split 23.35% to Peach State, which is $1,443.15, and 76.65% to Riverton Spine & Rehab, which is $4,736.77. Underneath, you can see $7,965.00 of liens hanging off the end in red hatching, and that little red card on the right says it all: John Doe nets $0.00. I call that red hatching the “so when's my check?” zone, because that's the question you'd be answering every day if this were the real file. Along the bottom is the order of work. Audit, correct, calculate, ask with authority, confirm in writing, and then the Net Sheet gets updated. The math is the leverage, and the audit always comes before the ask. {name}, read me the two percentages and tell me which lien carries more of the pain.
model.ask: {name}, why do we compute each share from the fraction instead of the rounded percentage?

job.say: On the job, it runs in three beats. When the provider's Final Ledger arrives, you audit each line against the visit records you requested, and you ask in writing for any error to be corrected. On John Doe's file, that's 33 visits matched, the 05/04/2026 duplicate removed, and $6,105.00 in the Lien Tracker. With the audited balance confirmed, you draft the Reduction Request with the math and get Atty. Thorne's written authority, escalated through CMS, logged before the request goes out or any call is made. And when a reduction is agreed, you get the signed Payoff Letter, update the Lien Tracker and the Net Sheet, and recompute the net that same day. A Case Manager I trained once won a gorgeous 30% off a provider bill, celebrated with the whole team, then found two duplicate visits on it. She'd negotiated a discount on money the provider was never owed. Audit first, celebrate second.
job.ask: {name}, which of those three beats would you be most tempted to rush, and what would it cost John Doe?

case.say: Something just landed, 10/06/2026, on PSH-55017742, and before I read it, a quick guess. {name}, which of John Doe's two liens do you think writes to us first? Here's the reveal: Peach State Health Plan. It asserts its reimbursement right of $1,860.00, paid for the 05/15/2026 epidural injection at Crescent Pain & Spine, and asks us to confirm its claim will be protected from the proceeds. The notice of rights and the EOB, the plan's statement of what it paid, are attached. Some context: Cardinal State has just tendered its $10,000 limits, so the gross is $40,000.00. Funny how a lienholder can stay quiet for months and then write the very week the money shows up. They always know. Both liens have been on the Lien Tracker since the pre-demand audit, and Atty. Thorne held the Reduction Requests until the gross was known. Now look at the plan documents. There's one word in there worth real money.
case.ask: {name}, what one fact about Peach State decides which law governs its claim?

task.say: Here's what you'll do, all in the Lien Tracker on the Net Sheet. Match the plan's itemized payments to the treatment record, classify the lien, record its funding status, and escalate the governing-law question to Atty. Thorne through CMS Tasks. Then draft the Reduction Request for his signature in Documents, Outgoing. Name the doctrine, show the one-third math down to $1,240.00, cite the work that built the fund, beating the 14-Day Gap defense with the MRI, and flag made whole as his to argue. Record every absent claimant as a verified none with its source. You'll hand in the request ready for his signature, a fully cleared Lien Tracker, and the 10/09/2026 acceptance at $1,240.00 once it's confirmed in writing. {name}, you're matching the EOB to the treatment record. {name}, you're on the absent claimants. And yes, you may use a calculator. Nobody in this office does one-third of $1,860.00 in their head and lives to brag about it.
task.ask: {name}, who decides whether John Doe was made whole, and what do you write down if a lienholder asks you?

model.say: Here's the reference model, a lab bench in two panels. On the left is the Lien Tracker with one live row, Peach State going from $1,860.00 to $1,240.00, with the math underneath: $1,860.00 times one-third is $620.00. Below it are the hollow rows, each stamped none, verified, with its source: BCRC, which is Medicare's recovery office, Medicaid verified, Harbor Point's 03/02/2026 letter, intake. On the right is the draft Reduction Request for Atty. Thorne's signature, with a red hold tag across the corner. And between them, an escalation to Atty. Elijah Thorne on governing law and doctrine. The point of the picture is who does what. You build the request. Counsel releases it. The bare-minimum version sends the request the minute it's typed. The high-value version waits for that tag to come off, because one letter sent without authority can cost the firm more than the whole lien. {name}, tell me what that red tag is protecting.
model.ask: {name}, what has to happen before that red hold tag comes off the request?

check.say: Before you log it, check yourself. Is the plan ledger matched to the one accident-related charge, the 05/15/2026 injection, $3,400.00 billed and $1,860.00 paid? The lien is what the plan paid, not what was billed. Is Crescent's $1,540.00 write-off recorded as not owed? Is the lien classified contractual, with fully insured status from the plan documents and the governing law recorded as Atty. Thorne's call? Is the common-fund math shown, citing the MRI and the 06/19/2026 Causation Letter? Are the absences complete, Medicare, Medicaid, hospital and workers' comp, each with date and source, the prior attorney as none known to John Doe, and PIP recorded as not a lien? And did you log $1,240.00 as final only with Peach State's written confirmation and Atty. Thorne's approval attached? That's where people trip.
check.ask: {name}, who checked Summit Imaging, which asked for an LOP on 03/11/2026?

why.say: Finish the sentence, fast, first thing that comes to mind: “A lien reduction isn't done until…” {name}, go. Somebody else? Okay, here's the reveal. Riverton Spine & Rehab has agreed to take less, and most people say the agreement is the finish line. It isn't. The finish line is the signed Payoff Letter. A reduction is won on paper first and on the phone second. The lienholder needs to see the audited balance, the recovery, the fee and costs, and the other liens, so it can see why taking less is fair. And it needs a letter it can sign that closes the bill for good. Skip the paper, and you either leave money on the table or reopen a bill you thought was closed. A verbal yes from a billing office is like a client saying “I'll fax it tonight.” Lovely to hear. Not something you can deposit.
why.ask: {name}, what goes to the lienholder before you ever pick up the phone?

doc.say: Before you ever pay a lien, meet the most important piece of paper in lien negotiation. {name}, guess what it is. The Payoff Letter. It's the lienholder's signed letter stating the agreed payoff in full satisfaction: no balance billing, which is billing the client for whatever's left, no collections, and a release of its lien. Its legal purpose is to put the reduction you won on the phone in writing, so once it's paid the account closes at $0.00 and John Doe isn't billed for it again. Its evidentiary role on our file is Riverton Spine & Rehab's letter of 10/12/2026: $6,105.00 audited, $4,580.00 accepted, as long as it's paid within 30 days. That letter is what backs the disbursement. Your handling is simple and strict. No Payoff Letter, no payment. Check every figure against the audited balance, docket the 30-day condition, and update the Lien Tracker and the Net Sheet the same day. The lazy version says "they agreed on the phone." Phone agreements have the shelf life of milk. The high-value version gets it in writing, because a deal you can't prove is a bill that comes back.
doc.ask: {name}, what happens to Riverton Spine & Rehab's balance if the $4,580.00 isn't paid within 30 days?

rules.say: Four rules carry this. First, you negotiate from the audited balance, never the billed one: Riverton at $6,105.00, Peach State at $1,860.00, $7,965.00 in all. Second, the written Reduction Request goes first, with Atty. Thorne's written authority already on file. Third, on the call you make his ask and nothing outside it, and you log the name, the date and every figure. A counter outside his authority goes back to him the same day. The lazy version is “they said they'd work with us.” The high-value version is “Tammy Greer, billing manager, offered this figure on this date, routed to Atty. Thorne at this time.” Fourth, no Payoff Letter, no payment, and the letter says full and final, with no balance billing or collections, meaning nobody can chase John Doe for the rest later. Then you update the Lien Tracker and the Net Sheet that day. {name}, which rule do you think gets broken most?
rules.ask: {name}, if the provider counters below Atty. Thorne's floor, what exactly do you say on the call?

job.say: Here's the job, start to finish. When the audited balance is confirmed, you draft the Reduction Request with the math and get Atty. Thorne's written authority before it goes. When the lienholder responds, you call with the authorized ask and log who you spoke to, when, and every figure. And when the reduction is agreed, you get the signed Payoff Letter, then update the Lien Tracker and the Net Sheet so John Doe can see his net change the same day. I had a client once who called every morning at 8:01 to ask, “So when's my check?” The day we sent him an updated Net Sheet showing his number going up, he stopped calling for a whole week. Clear paper is the best client service there is. Now your mystery. On BI alone, John Doe nets $0.00. On the real file, it's $20,359.92. {name}, before the next lesson, tell me what you think turned zero into twenty thousand.
job.ask: {name}, if a provider later says the bill is still open, which of these three steps would you check first?

case.say: It's 10/09/2026, and Peach State has accepted $1,240.00 in writing. One down. Now here's what just landed from Riverton Spine & Rehab: John Doe's Final Itemized Ledger under the 02/23/2026 Letter of Protection, 34 visits at $185.00, balance $6,290.00. They understand the case is settling and want to know when to expect payment in full. Notice they said payment in full. Providers and clients have the same favorite question this week, and it's “so when's my check?” Visit notes are attached. Atty. Thorne has set a target for Riverton in writing, and the Reduction Request is yours to draft. We're running this one live. {name}, you're making the call, and I'll warn you now, the billing manager is going to push back: “We gave him 33 visits on a promise of payment, and you want a discount?” Your answer is the audit and the true facts, not sympathy. And did you catch the number that doesn't match?
case.ask: {name}, she says 33 visits. So how many lines did Riverton actually bill?

task.say: First, audit Riverton's ledger against the visit records and request a written correction before you ask for anything. Then draft the Reduction Request for Atty. Thorne's approval, and send it once he approves. Next comes the follow-up call in the Call Simulator with Tammy Greer, the billing manager. State the audited balance, $6,105.00 with the 05/04/2026 duplicate removed. Explain the coverage-capped recovery as facts, and ask for payment in full in the interest of global resolution. She'll agree to $4,580.00 on the call. Accept nothing; it goes to Atty. Thorne. Ask for a signed Payoff Letter with full satisfaction and no balance billing. You'll hand in the logged call, the Payoff Letter dated 10/12/2026, and a recomputed Net Sheet showing $20,359.92. I once heard a brand-new Case Manager hear a yes on a call and shout “Deal!” so loud the whole office cheered. The attorney hadn't approved it. The cheering stopped. {name}, you're on the phone; {name}, you're logging every figure she says.
task.ask: {name}, the manager just said yes to $4,580.00. What are your exact next words?

check.say: Check yourself before you log it. {name}, did you audit line by line, 34 billed lines against 33 documented visits, 16 before the disruption and 17 after? Did you request the written correction for the 05/04/2026 duplicate before any reduction, taking $6,290.00 down to $6,105.00? No lines between 04/02 and 04/21/2026? Was the request approved and sent before the call? Did you argue only true facts, a recovery capped at $40,000 of coverage, and never claim the client would refuse? When she said $4,580.00, did you say it goes to Atty. Thorne and will be confirmed in writing? Is the signed Payoff Letter on file with full-and-final and no-balance-billing language? And does the Net Sheet show $20,359.92? The bare-minimum file has a number. The high-value file has a number, a letter and a log. That letter is what lets the 10/22/2026 disbursement go out clean. So here's the mystery: what would the error have cost if nobody had audited?
check.ask: {name}, if you'd opened with a discount on $6,290.00, how much error would you have negotiated around?

questions.say: This is the Lien Reduction Verification, and let's treat it like a quiz show where the grand prize is John Doe's net. Answer from the file, in your own words, typed under each question. Question one: classify each claim on John Doe's $40,000, that's Peach State, Riverton Spine & Rehab, PIP, Medicare and Medicaid, and a prior attorney, as statutory, contractual or none, and rank the liens by how far they'll bend. Question two: explain why Peach State being a fully insured group plan matters, and who decides what follows. That's the big one. If your answer is “state law applies, so we argue made whole,” you've just made Atty. Thorne's decision for him, and that's a buzzer. Question three: show the math from $1,860.00 to $1,240.00, name the doctrine, and connect it to beating the 14-Day Gap with the MRI. Calculators are allowed. Crying over the math is also allowed, quietly. {name}, you're first to submit, no pressure.
questions.ask: {name}, on question two, where exactly does your job end and Atty. Thorne's begin?

summary.say: Time for the Self-Summary. Put the principles of lien reduction into your own words, not the clicks. Then your strategy: with both liens resolved, what's the next action before the 10/22/2026 disbursement, and why is it the right one? Then name the one thing you're least confident about, and what would get you there. Before you write, glance at the scenario on screen, Keystone's 08/14/2026 release with Harbor Point's consent still out and Atty. Thorne away. A Case Manager I knew once got a call like that on a Friday at 4:55, “sign today or the offer's gone,” with the attorney on a plane. She didn't panic, she didn't sign, she documented it, called the attorney's cell, and left a written escalation. The offer was still there on Monday. It almost always is. Hold onto that instinct for every pressure question: stop, document, escalate. {name}, you'll read yours out first.
summary.ask: {name}, when a deadline and an absent attorney collide, what's the one thing you never do?

scale.say: Now the Skill Scale for this module. Rate yourself 1 to 5 on each skill, from classifying liens as statutory or contractual right through to holding the authority line in lien negotiation. I'll compare each rating with your score. If you gave yourself a 5 and scored 60, or a 2 and aced it, we'll sit down and talk about why. And remember, UPL, practicing law without a license, is a gate. No score survives an ethics breach. Submit when you're ready. Then here's a mystery to carry into the Final Accounting Check. A balance of $1,540.00 is going to turn up on John Doe's account. It's the exact gap between what Crescent billed and what Peach State paid. Is that a lien we missed, or a bill nobody owes? {name}, I want your gut answer now, and your proof from the file when we get there.
scale.ask: {name}, which lien skill felt strongest today, and does your score agree with you?

why.say: Two numbers on the board: $6,179.92 against $7,965.00. That's the BI stream alone. Quick game, closest guess wins bragging rights: what would John Doe have taken home? {name}, you first. Anyone else? The answer is nothing at all. Now here's what he actually nets: $20,359.92. The difference is why the Net Sheet matters. The Net Sheet, in plain words, is the one page that shows every dollar coming in and every dollar going out. Most people read a Net Sheet once, squint, and then just ask what the bottom number is. That's fine for the client. It's not fine for us. His $40,000 came from three carriers in two streams, and it goes out as five checks. The Net Sheet shows where every dollar came from and where it's going before a cent leaves trust. If you can't trace a dollar on the sheet, it doesn't move. And there's one trap on this sheet that catches even experienced people. I'll show you where it hides.
why.ask: {name}, what do you think turned $0.00 into $20,359.92 on this file?

theory.say: The Net Sheet is your tool for honesty and control, and it works in two streams. Think of two buckets. The first bucket is the third-party BI stream, the money from the at-fault driver's insurance company. Emptying that one first, all the way to its limit, is usually a legal step you have to take before you can touch the second bucket. The second bucket is the first-party UM stream, from the client's own policy or a relative he lives with, and it only opens once BI is used up or the driver has no insurance. Now the trap I promised: double-dipping, which means the same dollar gets counted twice. Carriers audit closely, so tracing every dollar's source keeps liens paid correctly and the buckets from mixing. And the final total puts both streams side by side, so the client sees what the work added. The lazy sheet is one long column. The high-value sheet is two clean ones. {name}, which would you rather defend to an auditor?
theory.ask: {name}, have you ever seen money counted twice on a bill or a paycheck, and how was it caught?

frame.say: Here are the two streams on John Doe's Net Sheet. Before I fill them in, {name}, guess how many insurance companies are feeding these two columns. Stream one is third-party BI, the at-fault driver's insurance company. You use up its limit first, because that's usually a legal requirement, and here it's Keystone, $10,000. Stream two is first-party UM or UIM, coverage from a host vehicle or a relative John lives with, which only kicks in once BI is used up or the at-fault driver is uninsured. On our file that's $20,000 from Harbor Point plus $10,000 from Cardinal State. So the answer is three. Keep them in separate columns from the first entry to the last, and you'll never have to untangle them later. I once watched a team spend an entire Friday untangling one sheet where somebody had mixed the streams on line two. By five o'clock, the calculator had more personality than they did.
frame.ask: {name}, why did Stream 2 only open after Keystone paid its full $10,000?

rules.say: Here are the rules, and where your role stops. One Net Sheet, two tabs. The Recovery Ledger carries money in and every deduction, and the Lien Tracker proves each lien figure. Neither is final until they tie out. Keep the streams apart, BI $10,000.00 and UM $30,000.00. PIP's $5,000.00 is a payment source on the Lien Tracker, never recovery. Price the fee per stream at 33⅓% pre-suit: $3,333.33 plus $10,000.00 is $13,333.33. Every cost needs a receipt, $486.75 in all, split 25% and 75%, $121.69 and $365.06. Reduce liens globally, then allocate pro rata. Run the net both ways: $5,089.98 plus $15,269.94 is $20,359.92. Flag future ESIs, which are injections, of $3,400 to $6,800 for Atty. Thorne. You build and explain the arithmetic. You never tell John Doe whether the net is enough. That one's tempting when he asks, “Is that good?” Your answer is the math, and Atty. Thorne answers the rest.
rules.ask: {name}, why does Harbor Point's PIP appear on the Lien Tracker but not in the gross?

model.say: Here's John Doe's Net Sheet, both tabs. The Recovery Ledger is in front, with three columns: total, Stream 1 BI and Stream 2 UM. Down the rows you've got the gross, the 33⅓% fee, costs, Peach State and Riverton Spine & Rehab, closing on that heavy orange net row: $20,359.92, which is $5,089.98 plus $15,269.94. See those thin orange lines running from each lien row back to the Lien Tracker tab? They read proved by Payoff Letter. And in the corner, the reminder that BI alone meant $0.00 to John Doe. Every figure on the net row traces back to its source. That's the whole idea. Here's the honest truth: nobody wants to read a Net Sheet twice. That's exactly why you build it so they only have to read it once. {name}, trace one line for me, out loud, from the net row back to its proof.
model.ask: {name}, if the two stream nets didn't add up to $20,359.92, where would you look first?

job.say: On the job, the Net Sheet builds as the file moves. Each settlement check that arrives gets posted to its stream on the Recovery Ledger, with carrier and check reference: BI $10,000.00, UM $20,000.00 plus $10,000.00, $40,000.00 total. Each cost gets its receipt attached and is posted once; five receipts make $486.75, and nothing is charged to both streams in full. When a lien reduction is accepted, the Lien Tracker gets the asserted, audited and reduced figures and the Payoff Letter: Peach State $1,240.00, Riverton Spine & Rehab $4,580.00, letters dated. And once both tabs are complete, you tie the Net Sheet to the Trust Ledger, net $20,359.92 on both, and route it to Atty. Thorne before John Doe ever sees it. Why does that order matter? Because the first number a client sees is the number he remembers forever. Show him a draft that's off by a hundred dollars, and you'll be explaining that hundred dollars until the day the file closes.
job.ask: {name}, why does the Net Sheet go to Atty. Thorne before John Doe ever sees it?

why.say: Remember that mystery line? Here it is, from Keystone's 08/14 draft, struck through: “all other persons, firms, corporations and insurers.” Quick vote: hands up if you'd have caught that on a first read. Keep them up if you'd have caught it at 4:45 on a Friday. Yeah. {name}, what do you think it would have cost John Doe if nobody had read it? $30,000. It would have released both UM carriers. A release, by the way, is the paper where the client gives up the right to sue in exchange for the money. That's why we audit every one. A settlement isn't over when a carrier says yes. It's over when the right release is signed, every check has cleared trust, every lien is paid off in writing, and the ledger reads $0.00. Until then, the work isn't done, no matter how many times the client asks, so when's my check?
why.ask: {name}, when any release lands on your desk, what's the first thing you read for?

doc.say: Before you audit one, let's break down the Limited Release, and I'll show you a sentence worth $30,000 in a minute. It's the document John Doe signs to end his BI claim, and it releases Robert Smith and Keystone only, for the $10,000, and nobody else. Its legal purpose is to end the claim against Smith in exchange for payment while preserving the UM claims against Harbor Point and Cardinal State. Its evidentiary role is exhaustion proof, proof the first policy has been paid out in full: signed 08/28/2026, it sits in each UM demand. Now the reveal. Look at what Keystone actually sent on 08/14: a release of all other persons, firms, corporations and insurers. {name}, how much coverage just disappeared? That's $30,000 of UM coverage. Your handling is to audit every line, quote the over-broad words in a redline memo, a memo marking exactly what's wrong, to Atty. Thorne, and hold any signature until both consents are in. What a clause means for John is his to explain. The lazy auditor skims for the dollar amount. The high-value one reads every "and" and "all," because insurers hide the expensive words in the boring sentences.
doc.ask: {name}, who are the other insurers on this file, and what would releasing them have cost John Doe?

theory.say: Here's the road from a signed deal to a ledger at zero. Audit the release line by line. Get both UM consents before the BI release is signed, meaning the UM carriers agree in writing first. Show John Doe how $40,000.00 becomes his net. Deposit each check to IOLTA, the firm's trust account for client money, the day its release is signed. And disburse on Payoff Letters and Atty. Thorne's signature until the ledger reads $0.00. Four documents close a case. The Release of All Claims ends the right to sue, and its wording decides which claims survive. The Settlement Disclosure Statement runs from gross to net and says full and final. A Satisfaction of Lien is the provider's signed letter that its lien is paid. And where suit was filed, a Dismissal With Prejudice means it can't be filed again. The lazy closer collects whatever paper shows up. The high-value closer knows the four by heart. {name}, name them back to me.
theory.ask: {name}, which of these four documents has John Doe's file not needed, and why?

frame.say: Here's the payout workflow, four stages, and each one protects accuracy, compliance and the client against fraud. Verification first: you review the Ready for Payment files and confirm every condition precedent is met, meaning every box that has to be ticked before money can move. Then documentation: you collect the invoices and receipts and make sure each one is readable and matches the claim. Then authorization: Atty. Thorne approves and signs, and the packet goes to accounting. You never sign it. And finally reconciliation: you confirm receipt of the funds and update the case file to show Paid. On John Doe's file, all four stages land between 10/20 and 10/22/2026. Why so strict? Because the scariest email in this business is the one that says “new bank details, please wire it here instead.” Scammers love settlement week. {name}, which of these four stages do you think stops that email?
frame.ask: {name}, which condition precedent on John Doe's file was the last to close before 10/22?

rules.say: Here are the rules, and where you stop. Read every release line by line before John Doe sees it: who's released, which claims, what he promises. A BI release can't reach what's still open, like the Civic's property-damage claim with Keystone PD, and both UM consents come before it's signed. The indemnity clause, which is John Doe's promise to repay the carrier if a lienholder later chases it, means every lien must be tracked and paid off in writing. Harbor Point's release must not reach Cardinal State. The Settlement Statement shows $40,000.00 becoming $20,359.92. Log each check on arrival, deposit to IOLTA once its release is signed, and never disburse before funds clear on 10/20. No suit was filed here, so no dismissal. You audit, flag, prepare and verify. Atty. Thorne explains, approves and signs. {name}, here's a test of that line.
rules.ask: {name}, Keystone's check is in. Why can't we pay Riverton Spine & Rehab today?

model.say: This is John Doe's money path, and no gate opens before the one to its left has closed. Gate one, the releases signed, 08/28 plus the UM releases. Gate two, the checks into IOLTA on 09/04, 10/05 and 10/13. Gate three, funds clear on 10/20. Gate four, the statement is signed on 10/21. Gate five, Atty. Thorne signs on 10/22. Gate six, reconciled to $0.00. Above gate one is that struck-through line again, with minus $30,000 beside it, and underneath, the Trust Ledger steps down from $40,000.00 to $0.00. So here's your answer: we can't pay Riverton until funds clear, the statement is signed, the Payoff Letter is in hand and Atty. Thorne signs. Think of it like an airport. You can't board just because you have a ticket. You still have to clear security, and nobody cares how loudly you tell them your flight is boarding. {name}, which gate would a client most want to skip?
model.ask: {name}, if someone pushed to pay one lienholder early, which gate would you point to, and why?

job.say: Here's how it runs on the job. When a settlement is agreed or tendered, request the payee's W-9, the tax form that lets accounting cut a check, the same day, and send it back with the signed release, so accounting never holds the check. When a carrier's draft release arrives, audit the parties, claims, indemnity, Medicare and confidentiality terms in the release audit, and route a redline memo; every over-broad line gets quoted and flagged before John Doe sees it. A redline memo is a short note that quotes each bad line of the draft, marks the fix and says what it would cost the client, like a teacher's red pen. When a check arrives, confirm its release is signed, deposit it to IOLTA that day and log the clearance date: 09/04, 10/05 and 10/13, $40,000.00, all cleared by 10/20. And if a suit is pending, which isn't Track A, you prepare the stipulation of dismissal with prejudice, docket it and confirm the court entry. Skip the W-9 step and you'll learn a lesson the hard way: a check can sit in accounting for two weeks over one missing form.
job.ask: {name}, which of these steps would you put on your calendar the very day a settlement is agreed?

dodont.say: Let's play Three Clues, One Rule. Three clues, you call Do or Don't, then name the rule. {name}, you're on the buzzer. In play: matching each document to its signer, the release to John Doe, the Payoff Letter to the lienholder, the W-9 to the payee, a dismissal to the attorneys. Secure e-signature or an in-person signing, with a current notary stamp and ID matching “John Doe” exactly. The Kickback Protocol: say exactly what's missing and give a deadline. It's called a kickback because the paperwork gets kicked back to whoever sent it, with a note that says exactly what's missing and by when. Cross-referencing invoice numbers, which is how we caught the 05/04/2026 duplicate. And the traps: a General Release that wipes out UM or the property-damage claim, checks against uncleared funds, payment instructions taken from an email without a phone check. And that indemnity clause? Not boilerplate. It's John Doe's promise that every lien gets paid. Now, the mystery for the next lesson. On 10/22 the Trust Ledger hits $0.00. {name}, is John Doe's file closed? Think hard before you say yes.
dodont.ask: {name}, what makes it safe for John Doe to sign that indemnity promise?

case.say: Here's what landed today, 10/13/2026. Cardinal State Mutual's $10,000.00 is deposited to IOLTA on CS-26-20355, but it hasn't cleared. That joins Keystone's check, received 09/04, and Harbor Point's, 10/05, each deposited only after its release was signed. Trust has received $40,000.00. Peach State accepted $1,240.00 on 10/09 and Riverton Spine & Rehab accepted $4,580.00 on 10/12, both in writing. Costs stand at $486.75. Both Net Sheet tabs are half-built, and they need finishing before the Settlement Statement is drafted. Now a riddle before you touch anything. There are two lines on this file that look like money we owe, and we owe neither. {name}, can you name them? Here they are: PIP's $5,000.00 and Crescent's write-off. Add either to the payables and you've paid John Doe's money away. It's like tipping twice because you forgot you already left cash on the table, except the money isn't yours.
case.ask: {name}, why isn't Harbor Point's PIP $5,000.00 paid back out of the settlement?

task.say: You're completing both tabs of John Doe's Net Sheet. On the Recovery Ledger, post each check by carrier and stream, the 33⅓% fee per stream, the five receipted costs, and costs and liens split 25% and 75%, down to the net per stream and in total. On the Lien Tracker, list every provider and payer with charges, payments, adjustments and balance owed, then each lien's asserted, audited and reduced figure, the basis of each reduction and its payoff-letter status. Tie both tabs to the Trust Ledger. You'll hand in a two-tab Net Sheet reaching $20,359.92 down both streams and across the total, with every lien figure proved and routed to Atty. Thorne. {name}, you're on the Recovery Ledger. {name}, you're on the Lien Tracker. Calculators out, and run every number twice. In this job, “I was close” is not a total. And think hard about what you flag before John signs, because one future cost isn't on either tab yet.
task.ask: {name}, if Riverton Spine & Rehab had accepted $4,580.00 only on a phone call, could the line be marked final?

check.say: Check the arithmetic both ways before you log it, and I'm calling names. {name}, gross: Keystone's $10,000.00 to Stream 1, Harbor Point and Cardinal State's $30,000.00 to Stream 2. Fee: $3,333.33 plus $10,000.00, $13,333.33. Costs: $486.75, split $121.69 and $365.06, charged once. Liens split 25% and 75%: Peach State $310.00 and $930.00, Riverton $1,145.00 and $3,435.00. Net: $5,089.98 plus $15,269.94 is $20,359.92, and $40,000.00 minus $19,640.08 lands in the same place. A one-cent drift means a stream got rounded on its own. I once spent an afternoon hunting one missing penny. Found it. Best day of my month. Are the zero-balance lines kept off the payables, with their sources? Is each lien's payoff status recorded, none final on a phone call? And the judgment call, the one future cost: did you flag up to $6,800 in possible repeat injections to Atty. Thorne before John Doe signs? Lazy files stop at the math. Great files see what's coming.
check.ask: {name}, why does the future-injection flag go to Atty. Thorne rather than straight to John Doe?

case.say: It's 10/21/2026, the day before the money moves. All three checks, $40,000.00, had cleared trust by yesterday, the last being Cardinal State's from 10/13. John Doe signed the Settlement Statement this morning. Both Payoff Letters are in Documents. And on Monday, 10/19, Vance & Kettering withdrew its lien in writing and Atty. Thorne released the hold. Disbursement is tomorrow. Your job today is to make sure that every gate behind the money is genuinely closed, and then to line up five commands that take the ledger to zero.
case.ask: {name}, who lifts a hold on trust money, and how do you prove it on the file?

task.say: Start with the conditions precedent, and check each one against its document, not your memory. Keystone's executed Limited Release and both UM releases. Cleared funds. The signed statement. The Payoff Letters. The prior-attorney lien withdrawn, with the hold released by Atty. Thorne. Then queue one disbursement command per Net Sheet line in the Trust Ledger for his approval: the fee and costs to the firm, Peach State, Riverton Spine & Rehab, and John Doe. Show the ledger reaching $0.00, and request the lien satisfactions and John's receipt with the payments. You'll also take John's call about his check.

check.say: Check it all before anything goes to Atty. Thorne. Are the executed Limited Release and both UM releases on file? Did funds clear by 10/20, and did John sign the statement on 10/21? Is the 10/19 withdrawal there, and the hold's release recorded as Atty. Thorne's? Do the five commands match the Net Sheet exactly: $13,333.33 fee, $486.75 costs, $1,240.00 to Peach State, $4,580.00 to Riverton Spine & Rehab and $20,359.92 to John Doe, totaling $40,000.00 and leaving $0.00? Is every packet complete, and is every command waiting for his signature, not yours?
check.ask: {name}, what would you do if the hold had not been released by 10/21?

questions.say: This is the Final Accounting Check. Let's play it like a quiz show with only one rule: no peeking at your notes on question one. Your answers come from this file, in your own words, typed under each question. Question one is the big one: take John Doe's $40,000.00 to his $20,359.92, stream by stream, with fee, costs and liens, and explain the 25% and 75% split. If you can't do that without notes, the Net Sheet isn't finished in your head yet, and that's okay, it means we practice. Question two: name the four document sets needed before the file is archived, the item on this file for each, and the retention period. Question three: after the 10/22/2026 disbursement the Trust Ledger reads $0.00. Which records prove it, and what would a leftover balance tell you? {name}, you look confident. You're up first.
questions.ask: {name}, can you carry $40,000.00 to $20,359.92 down both streams without looking at your notes?

summary.say: Now the Self-Summary, in your own words: the principles behind the Net Sheet, the release audit and the Trust Ledger. Then your next action between the $0.00 ledger on 10/22/2026 and the 10/30/2026 closing memo, and why. Before anyone writes, let's solve the mystery we've been carrying. A $1,540.00 balance, the gap between $3,400.00 and $1,860.00 on Crescent's injection, turns up on John Doe's account. {name}, lien we missed, or bill nobody owes? Look at Peach State's EOB before you answer. I once had a client bring in a bill like that, convinced the whole settlement was ruined. It turned out to be a billing office that hadn't applied the insurance write-off. Ten minutes on the phone, and it vanished. And keep the scenario on screen in mind. A deadline is never a reason to let John Doe sign a release that reaches $30,000 of UM coverage.
summary.ask: {name}, is this $1,540.00 a lien we missed, or a bill nobody owes, and which document proves it?

scale.say: Here's the Skill Scale for Net Sheets and closing. Score yourself 1 to 5 on each competency, from building a dual-stream Net Sheet that ties to the Trust Ledger, to holding the UPL boundary on releases, money and the client's questions. I'll put your rating next to your score, and any wide gap, high or low, is something we'll talk through together. As always, UPL is a gate, and a strong score doesn't survive an ethics breach. Submit it for review when you're done, and well done on Track A, the version of John Doe's case that settled. Now the mystery for the case that doesn't. Imagine Keystone had refused to pay its limit. No tender, no releases, no checks. {name}, what's the first thing that changes on John Doe's file, and whose calendar does it land on? That's where we're headed: the road to court.
scale.ask: {name}, looking back over Track A, which competency grew the most for you?

why.say: Two truths and a lie. One: adjusters love a 300-page stack of raw medical charts. Two: a missing document is a discount for the carrier. Three: we build the same package twice on John Doe's file. {name}, which one's the lie? Number one. Adjusters don't read 300 pages; they weigh them, sigh, and offer something small. Now the answer to our mystery. On 08/05/2026 Keystone offered $3,500 on a claim with $16,401.40 in Specials. The two reasons: the 14-day gap and a “degenerative” MRI, meaning they're calling it wear and tear from age, not the crash. That's what an adjuster does with any opening a package leaves. So today isn't about the demand letter; it's about everything behind it. Each part proves one thing: the bills, the story, the fault, the wages, and for the UM carriers, the coverage and the exhaustion. A part that's missing or sloppy is the adjuster's discount. We build it for the BI demand served 07/20/2026, and again for the UM demands that go out 08/31/2026.
why.ask: {name}, if you were Dana Whitfield, which part of a Demand Package would you open first, looking for a reason to pay less?

doc.say: Before you build the package behind it, let's break down the letter on top: the Time-Limited Demand. {name}, guess first: does a 30-day clock on a demand start the day we hit send, or some other day? Hold that. It's the firm's letter offering to settle John Doe's BI claim for Keystone's $10,000 per-person limit, open for a fixed time. Its legal purpose is to make Keystone decide on the record, on terms it can meet, and Atty. Thorne sets every one: payment of the $10,000, a Limited Release of Robert Smith and Keystone only, and Smith's affidavit of no other insurance as a condition. Its evidentiary role: emailed to Dana Whitfield on 07/20/2026 with 81 pages, Exhibits A through J, it proves exactly what Keystone had in hand. The thumbnail is the final as served; the faulty draft is yours to audit later. Now the reveal. The 30 days run from her written acknowledgement of receipt, her reply saying she got it, on 07/22/2026, so the window closes 08/21/2026. Not from the send date, and no certified mail: the sent email and her reply are the proof. The lazy version dockets from send and hopes. The high-value version logs the email, gets the acknowledgement in writing, dockets 08/21/2026 from it, and changes no term.
doc.ask: {name}, Dana's acknowledgement never arrives. What do you do that same day, and which date do you never docket from?

theory.say: A Demand Package is proof, sorted by what each piece proves. Each part answers one question the adjuster asks, and a missing part is her discount. First, the Big Four: Medical Specials, the Narrative, Liability Proof and Special Damages, all flawless before Atty. Thorne reviews. Plain words: the bills, the story, the proof of fault, and the other hard losses like wages. Second, the Human Story: how the injury changed John Doe's work and daily life, told only from his words and the records. Third, the weak file against the legal trap. Three hundred pages of raw charts and a letter that says our client hurts get a lowball; a two-page summary and a strict clock make refusing the limits risky. Fourth, documents by function: the UM package sorted into coverage, liability, special damages, general damages and the release. A template demand is like a birthday card signed “Dear Valued Customer.” Nobody feels a thing. {name}, which of the four feels most like a judgment call to you?
theory.ask: {name}, which of the Big Four do you think Keystone found weakest when it offered $3,500?

rules.say: Here's how you build it. Medical Specials come from line-item bills, meaning every visit and charge listed on its own line, reconciled to the audit: $14,817.40, with the 05/04/2026 duplicate gone, and every line carries its why. A two-page treatment summary goes in front of the records. The Human Story comes from John Doe's own words and the records: five shifts missed at Northgate, numbness into his right hand from 02/18, and that numbness and tingling, paresthesia, still there at MMI. You draft it, Atty. Thorne reviews it, and nobody dresses it up. Liability Proof is the Police Report, Ruth Calloway, the doorbell clip and the Property Damage photos. Special Damages is Northgate's $1,584.00 letter, for $16,401.40 in all. Then the Final Scrub: no overlaps, the 2021 low-back visits disclosed, every balance confirmed by phone. That's our last clean-up pass before anything leaves the building. The bare minimum is “all documents attached.” The high-value version ties every number out to the penny. For UM, rebuild by function, with exhaustion proof, not proof of uninsured status.
rules.ask: {name}, why is proof of uninsured status the wrong threshold document for John Doe's UM packages?

job.say: On the job it runs like this. When MMI is declared on 06/12/2026, you open the Demand Package task, request every provider's line-item bill, and ask John Doe how the injury changed his days, in his own words. In the week of service you run the Final Scrub: overlaps, the prior disclosed, and a call to every provider for its final balance, with a name and a date in the notes, until $16,401.40 ties out. Then you index every exhibit by what it proves and route the package and the narrative to Atty. Thorne. And once the Limited Release is signed on 08/28/2026, you rebuild each UM package by function, and the question of an impairment rating goes to Atty. Thorne, not to Dr. Reyes from you. An impairment rating is the doctor's number, usually a percentage, for how much permanent loss of function the client is left with, and only a doctor gives one. A rule of thumb from the field: if your cover letter needs its own table of contents, start over. Now your mystery for the negotiation lesson. Dana Whitfield is going to ask one question on the phone, six words long, and it's the question this whole file has to answer. {name}, guess it.
job.ask: {name}, why would a provider's final balance ever be different from the bill we already have?

case.say: Pop quiz, hands up. The insurance company says "we're tendering our limits." Who thinks that means the money is in our bank account? {name}, your hand's up proudly. Hold that thought. It's 08/12/2026, a Wednesday, and Dana Whitfield has just tendered Keystone's $10,000 BI limits, inside the 08/21 window. Tendered means offered, the whole policy, on the table. It does not mean received. Tendered is a promise; received is a check you can actually hold. Good news, and John Doe will hear about it soon. But no check has issued, no release is signed, and the UM layers haven't even been demanded yet. Atty. Thorne's memo asks for one thing before he sits down with John: the BI settlement Net Sheet, the page that shows where every dollar goes. Stream 1 on his 25% working allocation, and Stream 1 standing alone. The liens, the bills that get paid out of the settlement, are where they were on 08/05: Peach State at $1,860.00 and Riverton Spine & Rehab at $6,105.00 audited, nothing reduced. So picture John on the phone tomorrow saying Keystone paid ten thousand, where's my share. The answer is going to surprise him. It might surprise you too.
case.ask: {name}, if John Doe asks why he can't have his share of Keystone's $10,000 now, what does the math say?

task.say: You'll build Stream 1 in the LSH Net Sheet. {name}, you're on the keyboard; {name}, you're the calculator that checks the keyboard. Enter the $10,000.00 gross as tendered, not received. Take the fee at the pre-suit 33⅓% from the retainer, that's $3,333.33, and the five receipted costs, $486.75. Enter both liens as they stand today and leave the reduction column blank. Then run Atty. Thorne's 25% allocation, his split of costs and liens between the two streams: $121.69 of costs and $1,991.25 of liens, down to a projected net of $4,553.73, and label it a projection with what it assumes. Beside it, run the BI-alone fact pattern: $6,179.92 left against $7,965.00, shared pro rata, meaning each lien takes its fair percentage, and John at $0.00. Route it to Atty. Thorne today with the trust-hold flag. The allocation and anything about value are his. And if your calculator and your spreadsheet disagree by a penny, don't pick the one you like better. Find out why. That penny is where the real mistake lives.
task.ask: {name}, which figure on your sheet would you never read to John Doe, and why?

check.say: Check yourself before you route it, and I'm calling names. {name}, is the fee $3,333.33, and not $3,333.00 from typing 33.33%? Calculators are honest, but they're very literal. Are the liens $1,860.00 and $6,105.00, with no reduction pencilled in, because nobody has agreed one? Is Stream 2 open, with nothing entered? Is $4,553.73 marked as a projection, with the allocation and the open UM layers written beside it? Does the BI-alone pattern show $6,179.92 against $7,965.00, a $1,785.08 shortfall, Peach State $1,443.15 and Riverton Spine & Rehab $4,736.77, and John Doe at $0.00? And did you flag, as a fact, that the money can't be paid out on its own and stays in trust until the liens resolve, and leave the rest to Atty. Thorne? The lazy sheet has numbers. The excellent sheet tells Atty. Thorne which numbers are real and which are still hopes. Your mystery for the next activity: a $0.00 net today isn't the end of John's story. What would have to happen for that zero to grow?
check.ask: {name}, you posted Keystone's $10,000 to the Trust Ledger today. What's wrong with that entry?

case.say: Game time: firm or still moving. I'll read a number off John Doe's file, you shout "firm" if it's locked, "moving" if it can still change. {name}, you're the referee. It's the sixth of October. Teresa Okafor has just tendered Cardinal State's ten thousand dollar Relative UM limits, and John accepted through Atty. Thorne. UM, uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage, is the coverage that pays when the at-fault driver's insurance isn't enough, and Relative UM is the coverage John reaches through a relative's policy. Harbor Point's twenty thousand has been in trust since yesterday, and Keystone's ten thousand since the fourth of September. So the stack is closed at forty thousand, but only thirty thousand is actually in the account. Tendered still isn't received, and I'll keep saying it until you say it in your sleep. The liens haven't moved yet: Peach State asserts eighteen sixty, and Riverton Spine and Rehab's account is sixty-one oh five after our audit. Atty. Thorne's memo asks for the UM settlement Net Sheet before he goes through it with John. One of these numbers looks firm and isn't. Keep an eye out.
case.ask: {name}, of everything on this file today, which numbers are firm, and which are still going to move?

task.say: You're building Stream 2, the UM column, as it stands today. Post Harbor Point and Cardinal State to the Recovery Ledger, our running list of every dollar recovered and from whom, and show which check is in trust and which is only tendered. Take the pre-suit one-third fee. Then allocate costs and liens to Stream 2 at seventy-five percent, pro rata to gross, meaning in proportion to each check's size, with each lien at its asserted or audited figure, not the reduction you hope for. Hope is lovely. It's just not a column on the Net Sheet. Mark every figure that can still change, and write what will change it. Tie Stream 2 to Stream 1 and to the Trust Ledger, the firm's record of client money held in trust. Then the part I'm grading hardest: the questions Atty. Thorne has to answer before John sees this sheet. It goes to him, not to John. {name}, you're writing question one out loud for the room. {name}, you're writing question two.
task.ask: {name}, why does Stream 2 carry only seventy-five percent of the costs and liens, when it's the bigger check?

check.say: Check it to the cent, and {name}, you're reading the totals back to me. Gross thirty thousand. Fee ten thousand even. Costs: Stream 1 takes one twenty-one sixty-nine, so Stream 2 takes the remainder, three sixty-five oh six. Peach State, thirteen ninety-five. Riverton Spine and Rehab, forty-five seventy-eight seventy-five, on the audited figure, not the billed one. Projected net, thirteen thousand six sixty-one nineteen, labelled a projection. Add Stream 1's forty-five fifty-three seventy-three and you get eighteen thousand two fourteen ninety-two, which is forty thousand less the whole fee, the costs and the unreduced liens. If your two columns don't add up to that, your spreadsheet isn't broken, it's telling on you. Is Harbor Point's PIP at zero, with its 03/02 letter cited? Is Cardinal State receivable, not received? That's the number that looked firm and isn't. And are your four questions written down and routed today? Here's the mystery for the Learning Check: those liens haven't been reduced yet. Who decides whether they will be, and what on this sheet changes the moment they are?
check.ask: {name}, John calls tomorrow and asks if he's getting thirteen thousand. What do you tell him?

why.say: Here's the problem with Keystone's $10,000. The moment Harbor Point or Cardinal State pays John Doe, it steps into his shoes against Robert Smith. That right is called subrogation. If John releases Smith before those carriers agree, their right against Smith is gone, and the policy may let them refuse to pay. That's $30,000 of a $40,000 stack riding on two letters. So Keystone won't cut its check, and John won't sign anything, until both UM carriers consent in writing and waive subrogation. Bluewater, by the way, is not on that list. Margaret rejected UM on the Civic back on 03/14/2024, so there's nothing there to waive.
why.ask: Why would Keystone, the BI carrier, care whether the UM carriers waive subrogation?

doc.say: Now the paper itself, because a letter isn't enough here. {name}, quick question: if Harbor Point's adjuster leaves the company next year and this claim ends up in front of an arbitrator, how do we prove Harbor Point gave up its rights against Smith? We hand over the Waiver of Subrogation. It's a separate instrument from the consent letter, on the carrier's own form, signed by the adjuster and notarized. It waives Harbor Point's right to recover from Robert Smith and Keystone, and only them. It says the UM claim stays open, and that Harbor Point won't substitute its own check. Because it's sworn and acknowledged before a notary, it can be filed or offered as an exhibit without anyone having to come in and testify that the letter is real. Cardinal State signed its own on 08/26/2026, Harbor Point on 08/24. Your job: get the waiver itself, check it names the right carrier, policy and claim, check it covers Smith and Keystone only, and check the signature and the notary block are complete. What it waives, and what that means for John, is Atty. Thorne's to explain.
doc.ask: What can a notarized waiver do in court that a consent letter can't?

theory.say: Let me give you the four ideas behind this. Subrogation is the paying carrier's right to recover what it paid from the at-fault driver. The consent to settle is the UM carrier's written permission for John to settle with Smith and release him. Each carrier then has a choice: waive subrogation, or pay the $10,000 itself to keep its claim against Smith. On our file both waived and neither substituted, Harbor Point on 08/24 and Cardinal State on 08/26. And the fourth idea is Keystone's own payment condition: Dana Whitfield's 08/14 cover letter holds the check until both waivers arrive with the executed release.

rules.say: The rules are short. Ask the right carriers, which on this file means Harbor Point and Cardinal State, never Bluewater. The 30-Day Letter goes out the day after the tender, 08/13/2026, for Atty. Thorne's signature, with the tender letter and Smith's affidavit, and you docket each window. When a consent comes back, read what it covers: Smith and Keystone only, subrogation waived, no substitution. Anything wider, or a substitution offer, goes straight to Atty. Thorne. And John Doe signs nothing until both are in writing and Atty. Thorne has approved the release and gone through it with him. You request, docket, chase and match. You never explain the consent clause to anyone.

job.say: On the job it runs in three beats. Keystone tenders on 08/12/2026, and you prepare both consent requests for Atty. Thorne's signature and docket the windows; they go out 08/13 with the reason Bluewater isn't asked written on the file. On 08/14 Keystone's cover letter makes payment conditional on the waivers, so you log that condition and hold the signing task against it. Then the consents land, Harbor Point on 08/24 and Cardinal State on 08/26, and you match each one's scope to the release. Both cover Smith and Keystone only, so both go into the transmittal packet and the front of each UM package.

case.say: It's Friday, 08/14/2026. Keystone tendered its $10,000 on Wednesday, and our consent requests went to Harbor Point and Cardinal State yesterday. Today Dana Whitfield sends Keystone's own release form for John Doe's notarized signature. Her cover letter says the check won't issue until both UM carriers' consents and subrogation waivers arrive with it. Our demand asked for a Limited Release of Robert Smith and Keystone only. What landed is called a Release of All Claims. Before John Doe sees a word of it, we read every clause against what was promised and what's still open on this file.
case.ask: What's the first difference you'd expect between a Release of All Claims and the Limited Release we demanded?

task.say: Here's your job. Open the audit workbench and call every clause of Keystone's draft: keep, replace, pull, add, or flag for Atty. Thorne. For each one, write what it would do on this file and the amendment you'd propose. Then email your review to Atty. Thorne for approval, with the clauses that are his to decide clearly flagged. Don't send the draft to John Doe. When Dana Whitfield writes asking whether John can just sign the standard form now, you'll route that, not answer it. Finally, convert the whole exchange into a memorandum and file it in the CMS and on your Backup Drive.

audit.say: This is the audit itself, fifteen items. Some are the easy keeps: the parties, the $10,000.00, non-admission, the notary block. Then the ones that cost money. The catch-all reaching all other insurers would release Harbor Point and Cardinal State, $30,000. Property Damage and Loss of Use reaches the Civic's claim, which is Margaret's and still open, handled by Leah Moran. There's no UM reservation, a confidentiality clause nobody agreed to, an indemnity clause with no ceiling, and no payment date. And three clauses aren't yours at all: unknown injuries, the Medicare representation, and governing law. Those you flag.
audit.ask: Why can't the release stay confidential on this particular file?

check.say: Check yourself before you hand it in. Did you replace the catch-all and say exactly what it would release? Did you cut the claims back to bodily injury and add a reservation of both UM claims by claim number? Did you pull confidentiality, narrow the indemnity to the liens on the file paid from trust, and add a payment date for Atty. Thorne to set? case.say: It's Wednesday, 08/26/2026. Cardinal State's consent and waiver came in today, joining Harbor Point's from Monday. Keystone issued its Limited Release on 08/19, exactly as Atty. Does the ID match John Doe exactly, is the original wet-ink and notarized, every page initialed? Did the packet go to Keystone on 08/28 with both waivers and the W-9, and did you ask for written confirmation of receipt and the check date? case.say: It's Wednesday, 10/14/2026. The $40,000.00 is in trust, both liens are reduced in writing, and disbursement is set for 10/22. Then an email arrives from a firm none of us has heard of, Vance & Kettering Injury Law. task.say: Here's the work. Log the notice the moment it arrives and route it to Atty. Thorne the same day, and send nothing back to Vance & Kettering, not even to say no. On his instruction, put a temporary hold on the disputed $6,666.67 in the CMS and update the Action Plan so everyone sees the 10/22 disbursement depends on it. Then investigate. Pull their agreement, compare its signatures with John's own, line its date up against our engagement, and audit the work they claim. Call John Doe and ask, neutrally, whether he ever hired them. Deliver the packet to Atty. Thorne and archive everything in the CMS and Drive.

audit.say: In the workbench you'll test each claim in their notice against the file. Their agreement is the key exhibit, so you keep it whole, and it shows something important: the only signature is Margaret Doe's, as mother, and John's line is blank. You add what the notice leaves out: John's own signatures from 02/09/2026, a timeline showing we were engaged and had served the demand before 07/27, his account in his own words, and the hold record. You replace their claims of substantial services and carrier notice with what the record actually shows: 0.6 hours with Margaret and no carrier contact. And you flag the fee, the lien and their request for your confirmation.

check.say: Before you hand the packet over, check it. Was the notice logged and routed on 10/14, with nothing sent to the firm? Is the $6,666.67 hold in place on Atty. Thorne's instruction, and does the Action Plan show it? Did you compare the signatures and cross-reference the dates against 02/09 and 07/20? Did you quote their time record rather than characterize it? Is John Doe's account in his words, with no view from you on the lien? case.say: It's 07/17/2026, three in the afternoon. The pre-demand audit closed on Wednesday, and the demand to Keystone goes out Monday. In the last two weeks three documents were corrected: the MRI got an addendum fixing the history, Crescent sent a corrected statement down to zero, and the wage record went from a draft worksheet to a final. task.say: Here's your job: a backup audit before the demand goes out. Open My Backup Drive and compare the count of documents backed up with what's filed in the CMS. Any gap, back it up from Work From. Then the corrected documents. The current version goes in its folder, and the version it replaces stays right beside it, renamed SUPERSEDED with the date of the version that replaced it. Nothing gets deleted. The MRI addendum in Medical Records, Crescent's corrected statement in Bills, the final wage record in Wages and Costs. Then file the draft demand and the exhibit packet so they land in Insurance, Demands and Negotiation, labeled DRAFT. Run Check my drive, and record the audit in Case Notes. Lazy: eyeballing folders. High value: the CMS list, one document at a time.

check.say: Before you move on, check yourself. {name}, what's your X of Y? They should be the same number. Are the three current versions in Medical Records, Bills and Wages and Costs? Is every old version still there, labeled SUPERSEDED with a date? Are the draft demand and packet in Insurance, Demands and Negotiation, marked DRAFT? Did Check my drive come back clean?
